91:T19db,## Problem

`plugins/plugin-slack` handles `reaction_added` / `reaction_removed`, but the handlers took `_event`, **threw the reaction data away**, and emitted only the plugin-local `SLACK_REACTION_ADDED` / `SLACK_REACTION_REMOVED` with `buildEventPayload(accountId)` — a payload carrying no emoji, no user, no message reference.

Nothing in core consumes those plugin-local names. So Slack emoji signal never reached the agent at all: a consumer that wanted to count 👍/👎 had to poll `reactions.get`.

`plugin-discord` already bridges reactions to core's `EventType.REACTION_RECEIVED`. This PR gives Slack the same core-event contract, so a consumer counts reactions without knowing which platform produced them.

## Change

New `plugins/plugin-slack/src/reaction-bridge.ts`, wired into **both** reaction handlers on the real registered path (`app.event("reaction_added" | "reaction_removed")` in `registerEventHandlers`) — not a helper that could drift onto dead code.

- **Core contract matched exactly.** Emits `[SLACK_REACTION_ADDED, EventType.REACTION_RECEIVED]` on add, with a `MessagePayload` carrying the reaction `Memory`, mirroring `plugin-discord`'s `handleReaction`.
- **Same rooms as messages.** Reuses the service's own `createUniqueUuid` / `stringToUuid` helpers (`slack-room`, `slack-user`, `slack` keys, account-scoped) via an injected host adapter, so reactions land on identical room/entity UUIDs rather than a parallel set.
- **Thread recovery.** A Slack reaction event carries `channel` + `ts` but *never* `thread_ts`, so naive mapping drops every threaded reaction into the parent channel room, detached from the message it reacted to. The bridge resolves the target message memory (its id is deterministic from `ts`) and reuses its `roomId`, falling back to the channel room when the agent never saw the message.
- **Payload:** emoji name, mapped room UUID, reactor entity UUID, target message ref (`targetMessageTs` + deterministic `targetMessageId`, plus `content.inReplyTo`), resolved reacted-to text when known.
- **Back-compat preserved.** `SLACK_REACTION_*` still fire, now with the populated payload the `SlackReactionPayload` type always declared but never filled in. `SlackReactionPayload` now extends `MessagePayload` so one payload satisfies both event names.

### Deliberate: removal does not reach core

Core declares exactly one reaction event, `EventType.REACTION_RECEIVED` (`packages/core/src/types/events.ts`); there is no `REACTION_REMOVED`. `plugin-discord` resolves this by emitting `[DiscordEventTypes.REACTION_RECEIVED, EventType.REACTION_RECEIVED]` on add but only `[DiscordEventTypes.REACTION_REMOVED]` on remove.

We match that rather than "improving" on it. Emitting `REACTION_RECEIVED` for a Slack removal would make a platform-agnostic vote counter **double-count on Slack and not on Discord** — worse than the missing event. Removals still get the full enriched payload on `SLACK_REACTION_REMOVED`. Closing the asymmetry properly means adding `EventType.REACTION_REMOVED` to core and updating both plugins together; that is a core-types change, deliberately out of scope.

Likewise the bridge does not call `createMemory` itself — core's `reactionReceivedHandler` persists the reaction memory, same as Discord — so an add is stored once and a removal is not stored at all.

### Note on the room-mapping test

The room-mapping assertion initially passed vacuously: the harness stubbed `runtime.getRoom` with a blanket `mockResolvedValue({ id: "room-existing" })`, which made `ensureRoomExists` short-circuit on its `getRoom(roomId)` hit and return a room whose id never came from `createUniqueUuid` — so the mapping under test was never exercised. Replaced with a real room store keyed by UUID, so an unseen channel misses, falls through to the real `getRoomId` + `createRoom` path, and the test now additionally asserts `createRoom` was called once with the expected id/channel/source.

92:T16f0,Fixes #17466.

## Root cause

`#17436` correctly propagated transport cancellation into unfinished chat work, but several post-operation `throwIfAborted()` checks could discard a result that had already returned successfully. In the conversation SSE path that leaves no bound terminal outcome, releases the `clientMessageId`, and lets the reconnect execute and bill the completed turn again. The same ordering risk affected local-direct model results, direct pre-handler replies, and committed direct actions.

Removing those checks exposed a second boundary: `handleMessage` can return an executable fallback action payload. Its model result must survive a late disconnect, but the API must not interpret that completed result as permission to start a new fallback action after cancellation. The repaired boundary preserves completed work, fails unstarted fallback actions closed, and continues only pure/durable finalization.

A deeper audit found that action effect receipts were transient results, not durable replay records: if a planner or shortcut action settled and `DefaultMessageService` later aborted or threw, the route still had no outcome to bind and could repeat the external effect. The executor now publishes a privacy-projected settlement checkpoint synchronously at the handler completion barrier, before event emission or disclosure revalidation. The route uses applied receipts, terminal reconciliation results, or mutation capability tags as fail-closed proof; only receipt-verified text is replayed exactly.

Confirmed develop failures:

- [Tests run 30651472223, Server Tests job 91225793055](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/30651472223/job/91225793055)
- [Tests run 30656416185, Server Tests job 91243170836](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/30656416185/job/91243170836)

Both failed the same `conversation-idempotency` assertion: 21/22 passed, while `completed turn survives transport disconnect` observed two `handleMessage` calls.

## Change

- Preserve successful message/model/pre-handler/action returns across late transport cancellation so persistence and exact-key replay complete once.
- Never start fallback actions after cancellation; guard both action validation and the real handler so a cancellation racing during preflight cannot cross the execution boundary.
- Fail an unstarted fallback payload closed with an explicit durable `No side effects were applied` outcome, which reconnects replay without another model turn.
- Skip optional post-result work after cancellation: fallback/direct-action voice models, synthetic `MESSAGE_SENT` hooks, and exact-document lookup. Required persistence/idempotency finalization remains transport-independent.
- Keep cancellation checks before local-command work and after paths report `not handled`; unfinished message/pre-handler work still receives the owner signal.
- Thread settled-action checkpoints through planner execution, deterministic planner fallback, nested planner calls, and `runShortcutGate`; sensitive and owner-exclusive payloads remain projected.
- Persist a terminal conversation outcome when later message-service work aborts or throws after a mutating action settles, preventing same-key retries from repeating the side effect.

95:T12b3,## Problem

Four sub-agent lifecycle defects observed live on a production bot:

1. **App-build verify false-failed on third-party sub-resources**: reachability probing treated cross-origin/preconnect assets (font CDNs) as the app being down.
2. **Task-completion message spam + retry storms**: TaskSupervisor digests re-fired on permanent delivery failures, and completion residual checks flagged spawn-time dirt as the agent's changes.
3. **Coordinator wiring gave up at 90s**: a one-shot deadline where an open-ended poll (with backoff) is correct — long provisions were falsely orphaned.
4. **Inner monologue leaked to chat**: for a *stopped* claude task, swarm synthesis relayed the newest workdir transcript's LAST assistant text verbatim — for an interrupted session that's mid-task narration ("Now let me read the launch check itself…", relayed to a real user's Discord). Root-caused forensically: replaying the reader against the stopped session's jsonl reproduces the exact leaked string.

## Fix

- Verify treats third-party sub-resource failures as degraded, not dead (with a cross-origin degrade test).
- Digest damping: yields to the completion relay, stops retry-storms on permanent failure; residuals baseline captures spawn-time dirt.
- Coordinator wiring polls open-ended with slow-phase backoff instead of a one-shot deadline.
- **Status-keyed lifecycle relay** (never text-matched): a non-`completed` task relays its verification verdict when present, else "<task> — <status> before completion."; the transcript tail and raw lastOutput never relay. Completed tasks are untouched — a cleanly finished run's final message IS the user-facing result.

## Testing

- server-helpers-swarm suite **20 pass** — the new regression tests seed the REAL reader path (`~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-workdir>/` jsonl) with narration and prove it stays out of routed text; mutation-checked (gate removed → both fail). Seeded dirs are cleaned up after each test.
- Orchestrator suite **2622 pass**; the 2 remaining failures are a pre-existing env-sensitive test that fails identically on pristine develop (verified by baselining this exact environment against `origin/develop`).
- Live: the leak reproduced on a stopped app-build session pre-fix; post-fix restarts + builds produce lifecycle/verdict messages only.

96:Tcc1,## What

From the verified resilience audit (#17253 §1, `high`): the orphan-container reconciler keys a container on the id embedded in its **name**, and a container claimed from the warm pool keeps the name it was born with — `agent-<pool id>` — while the pool row that id points at is **deleted at claim time**. Resolving node-side keys against the primary key alone therefore maps every warm-claimed customer container to a deleted row, and the sweep classifies the **default happy-path container** as `no_db_row` and force-removes it mid-conversation, logged as a routine reap.

What has spared production so far is only that the reconciler is gated off by default (`ORPHAN_RECONCILER_ENABLED`). Arming it on any environment with warm pool enabled would delete live customer containers.

## Fix

Two layers:

1. **Key resolution** (`docker-node-workloads.ts`): `loadSandboxStatusesByIds` now also matches `warm_claim_source_pool_id` — which `claimWarmContainer` already persists on the claimed row — and mirrors every placement protecting that row (primary and replacement) onto the pool key. The container's name now resolves to the live row that owns it.

2. **Grace on `no_db_row`** (`orphan-container-reconciler.ts`): the same lesson `wrong_node` already learned from its prod dry-run (a 29-second-old container judged against a 12-day-old row): the container itself must be older than the grace window, and an unknown container age never reaps. What an orphan looks like is also what an in-flight creation looks like from the wrong side of a commit. An orphan is permanent — it can wait five minutes to be provably one.

## Tests

`40 pass / 0 fail` across the three suites (bun:test, CI-pinned 1.3.14). Verified fail-on-base by stashing the source changes: **6 fail** on the previous code — the PGlite loader tests (real `pushSchema` schema, real `loadSandboxStatusesByIds`, claimed row whose pool id resolves to a live placement on the right node, replacement placement mirrored, and the true-orphan case still yielding nothing), plus the grace cases (young container kept, unknown age kept, no clock kept).

Existing fixtures were aged (`createdAtMs: 0` + explicit `nowMs`) so every historical reaping decision is preserved and asserted unchanged.

# Background

A clean boot could report settled health after service startup failed. The failure was logged and converted to `null`, late plugin schema work could race service startup, and scheduling seeded tasks before its runner was registered. Those independent paths made broken initialization look healthy.

This change makes boot state transactional and observable:

- Service startup failures are typed, reported with plugin/service context, and retained in structured boot health.
- Handler and service registration roll back when startup/finalization fails.
- Late plugin registration serializes schema work before starting dependent services.
- Scheduling registers its runner structurally before the seed service runs.
- Personal-assistant scheduling contributions use the shared scheduling service boundary.
- Health and readiness distinguish pending, successful, and failed service initialization.

# Risks

Medium-high. This changes core plugin/service lifecycle ordering and intentionally turns formerly hidden initialization failures into unhealthy readiness. The added rollback and real PGlite integration coverage protect the affected paths, but final packaged fresh-state boot logs remain an explicit draft gate.

98:T1a90,## Problem

Live incident (production Discord bot, trajectory `tj-69d82bb89ebb69`): asked **"how many times have i mentioned bitcoin in this channel?"**, the agent replied *"i don't see any mention of bitcoin in the recent messages i can see."* — answering a beyond-window history question from the ~20-message visible window, and denying a capability it has.

Root cause is a **false capability denial baked into the Stage-1 prompt**, which the model obeyed faithfully:

1. `createV5MessageContextObject`'s `current_turn_boundary` instruction hardcoded *"the prior_message blocks are the only window you have, and there is no separate chat-history search tool."*
2. `messageHandlerTemplate` scripted the matching canned denial for a window miss.

But the runtime **does** have that tool: the `MEMORY` action's `op:search` filters the stored `messages` record by room + query. Because Stage-1 never sees the action catalog (only the `available_contexts` list), the routing hints on that action could never reach this decision — the turn ended at Stage-1 with `contexts:["simple"]`, no `toolSearch`, no planner, no tool. The hardcoded denial also directly contradicted two of the template's own rules (`never deny a capability when a context is available`; `never simple when … "how many X"`).

## Fix

The boundary instruction now branches on the turn's **actual capability surface** — whether the role-filtered `availableContexts` (already passed by every caller) includes the `memory` context:

- **Memory context present:** state that the visible blocks are the most recent window of a longer stored conversation, and route beyond-window recall/count questions to the memory context (`requiresTool`) so the stored record is actually searched. Every anti-fabrication guarantee is retained verbatim (never claim a search a tool did not return).
- **Memory context absent:** the previous text is **byte-identical** (verified: 1161 chars, string-equal), preserving the 2026-05-25 fabricated-search guard for minimal runtimes and sub-USER roles.

Supporting: the template's canned denial defers to the ground-truth capability rule instead of dictating "no such tool", and the `memory` context catalog description names conversation recall so Stage-1 can select it. The recent-messages provider also names its window (`most recent N`) rather than presenting itself as the whole conversation.

**No user-message-text inspection anywhere** — the branch reads only the registered, role-filtered context surface. (A prose-regex intent gate was removed as a bug in #17500; this deliberately does not reintroduce that pattern.)

### Known trade (raised in adversarial review)

The gate proves *context registration*, not *action registration*: `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_DEFINITIONS` seeds `memory` in core, while the MEMORY action ships in `@elizaos/agent`. A deployment building on `AgentRuntime` with custom plugins and no memory action would get the escalating branch. Two things bound the damage: the Stage-1 catalog **already** advertises the memory context on exactly those runtimes (the boundary now merely agrees with the catalog the model already sees), and the anti-fabrication rule still forbids claiming an unrun search — so the degraded outcome is one wasted planner escalation with an honest reply, not a fabricated answer. Tightening the gate to also require a registered memory-context action is a reasonable follow-up; it would diverge the boundary from the catalog, so it belongs with catalog action-gating rather than here. Happy to make that change if preferred.

## Testing

- Two new tests in `message-runtime-stage1.test.ts` assert the rendered Stage-1 prompt for both branches; the memory-branch assertions fail on pre-fix code by construction (the removed sentence exists verbatim in develop; the new strings exist nowhere pre-fix).
- Suites green: stage1 **104**, prompts **38**, context/catalog/registry/renderer **63**, message + planner lanes **121**, provider lanes **40**. `tsgo --noEmit` clean, biome clean on all touched files.
- Adversarial review verified byte-identity of the untouched branch, all three call sites of `createV5MessageContextObject`, no prompt-cache regression (the boundary event is `stable:false`, so the KV-prewarmed stable prefix is unaffected), and that guest/stranger turns keep the old denial via role filtering.
- **Live before/after on a production Discord bot** — see evidence.

9a:T1911,## Problem

A "make me a tiny app" request on a live bot exposed a chain of defects that made first builds slow, leaky, or falsely failed — measured live at 192s+ with a wasted 67s retry loop, versus ~71s clean:

1. **Unwinnable creates**: fresh directory scaffolds have no runtime launcher (the worker host executes plugin exports only), so the `full` profile's launch/browser checks failed by design → every create burned its retry budget and reported "stopped" for apps that were fine.
2. **Stale deploys**: the builder's own deploy step is model-ordered; a live build (`comet-catch`) copied dist **6 seconds before its final rebuild** and shipped the scaffold placeholder while the real app sat in `dist/`.
3. **Planner-loop failure authority ate completion proofs**: `plannerToolOperationKey` keyed failures on ALL params including the free-text `description` — models re-narrate retried commands, so logically-resolved failures stayed authoritative and the terminal `APP_CREATE_DONE` REPLY was replaced with the generic fallback → verification failed on proof-missing while every check passed.
4. **Vite base-path**: the scaffold's default absolute `/assets/` paths 404 under a `/apps/<slug>/` deploy prefix (white-screened pages); the dead-sub-resource retry prompt misdiagnosed it as "missing files", so retries could never fix it.
5. **Sentinel option values**: planners emit `editTarget:"None"` (stringified absent); treating it as a real edit target sent creates down the strict edit path into a cold-registry timeout.
6. **Chat jargon**: verifier status lines ("App verification passed."), duration parentheticals, and machine proof lines reached the user.

## Fix

- New `build` verification profile (typecheck+lint+test+build) for fresh scaffolds; edits of scaffold-marked workdirs use it too; installed launchable apps keep `full`. The `build` profile **requires the structured proof** like `full` (review finding: self-reported success must not skip it).
- **Authoritative publish**: opt-in via `APP_PUBLISH_DIR`/`APP_PUBLISH_URL_BASE` settings (or `ELIZA_APP_PUBLISH_*` env) — the create prompt carries a deploy contract (relative-base build, copy, HTTP 200 + asset 200 checks, live URL in the completion), and `verifyProject` itself re-publishes the fresh dist after a pass as a recorded `publish` check. A failed copy fails the run; a stale page can no longer pass.
- `plannerToolOperationKey` excludes the free-text `description` narration param (red-green regression test pins the incident shape).
- Scaffold template ships `base: "./"`; the retry prompt names the base-path diagnosis with the exact dead URL.
- `readOptionalRefOption` filters `"None"/"null"/"undefined"` for reference-style options only (the shared `readStringOption` keeps literal `"none"` — a legitimate settings/color value; review finding).
- Chat surface: one clean ack ("Building X now — I'll post the link once it's live."), one final casual line with the live URL; pass verdicts and machine proof lines never post.

## Testing

- app-control **1628** pass + tsc clean; core failure-correlation suite **12** (incl. the new narration regression, red on old code); coordinator/sanitizer suites green on the integrated branch.
- **Live ladder on a production Discord bot** (all URLs independently probed 200): lavalamp **79s**, kaleido **97s**, snowglobe **71s**, neonpulse **65s**, comet-catch (game, real test failure caught by the verifier and fixed by the builder mid-run) **235s** — final arc is exactly two messages: ack → "your app's live: <url>". Freshness proven post-fix: bubblepop deployed with zero scaffold-placeholder content.

9d:T112c,## Problem

The Stage-1 message prompt placed volatile provider output, especially CURRENT_TIME, before the large append-only conversation tail. Cerebras caches exact 128-token prefix blocks, so this ordering invalidated almost the entire reusable prefix every turn. The live Gemma 4 baseline reused only 41.57% of prompt tokens at p50 despite a stable system prompt.

The latency harness also summarized wall/model/provider time without preserving the exact production model input or provider-reported prompt-cache and queue timings. That made a green-looking report possible without proving what the model actually received.

## Fix

- Keep the stable system prompt first, then order the user message as current-turn boundary, chronological prior dialogue, volatile provider output, and the final current message.
- Preserve the semantic current-turn invariant without positional above/below wording.
- Capture the exact RESPONSE_HANDLER input for every warmup, sample, and cancellation invocation, including prompt segments and cache options but only allow-listed fields.
- Report prompt, cached, uncached, and cache-rate token distributions from Cerebras usage; missing cache telemetry is an explicit error rather than a fabricated zero.
- Preserve privacy-safe nested cached-token and provider time_info fields in the cloud probe.
- Give every related direct, gateway, and paired request a stable prompt_cache_key.
- Add observations only. There is no latency or cache threshold, ratchet, timeout gate, or changed-production-code test policy.

Fixes #17509

  lost or double-billed turn — and the persist-once guard is regression-tested.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

**A barge-in silently erased the exchange from the agent's memory.**

`bridgeSharedMessageStream` persisted a turn **only** on the model stream's
`finish` part. Any interruption before that — a voice **barge-in** cancelling
the SSE consumer, a client disconnect, or an upstream stream drop — unwound the
stream without writing anything, so the user's utterance never reached
`saveSharedRuntimeHistory`.

Voice and text chat read the **same** shared-runtime history for a room. So the
human spoke, heard the agent start answering, interrupted — and both the
question and the partial answer vanished from the transcript that text chat and
the next voice turn read back. Barge-in is the signature voice interaction, so
the most natural way to use voice was the way that lost your data.

This persists the turn on the interrupt paths too:

- the user's utterance is **always** kept (it was really said);
- any partial reply is kept as an assistant turn flagged `interrupted: true`, so
  later context knows it is a fragment, not a finished thought — honest context
  instead of either amnesia or a fabricated-complete reply;
- a **persist-once** guard shared with the `finish` path means a completion
  racing an interrupt cannot double-write;
- a failed recovery write is logged, never masked.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix (non-breaking).

# Documentation changes needed?

No. The behaviour change is described in code comments at the persistence seam.

# Risks

Low, and strictly in the safe direction: the retain budget only ever gets **smaller** (256 MiB → 128 MiB), never larger. Nothing that restores today stops restoring; what stops is retaining a payload that could never be restored. Small manual/auto v1 backups are untouched, and no heap or body limit is raised (the issue's rejected-shortcuts list is respected).

# Background

## What does this PR do?

The production canary failed because Cloud **retained** a snapshot larger than anything on the restore path can **consume**:

| Side | Constant | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| retain | `SNAPSHOT_MAX_RAW_BYTES` (`eliza-sandbox.ts`) | **256 MiB** | canonical (128 MiB), env-clamped |
| restore | `MAX_BACKUP_BODY_BYTES` (`packages/agent/src/api/server.ts`) | 128 MiB | canonical |
| reconstruct | `MAX_RECONSTRUCTED_BACKUP_CHAIN_BYTES` (`agent-sandboxes.ts`) | 128 MiB | canonical |

A 128–256 MiB snapshot was therefore retained, authorized a cutover, and could never be restored.

- New `packages/shared/src/agent-backup-limits.ts` holds **`MAX_RESTORABLE_AGENT_BACKUP_BYTES` (128 MiB)** — the one canonical v1 restorable wire size. `@elizaos/shared` is already a dependency of **both** `packages/agent` and `packages/cloud/shared`, so retain, restore and reconstruction import one source of truth with no import cycle. This mirrors the existing `chat-upload-limits.ts` precedent (a leaf limits module both sides import so they cannot drift).
- `resolveRetainableAgentBackupBytes()` resolves the `ELIZA_SNAPSHOT_MAX_RAW_BYTES` operator override **clamped to the canonical limit**. The override keeps its real purpose (lowering the budget for a staging soak or a constrained worker) but can no longer re-open the divergence by configuration alone — which it could before.
- The breach still fails exactly where it already did: **while streaming, before retention** (`readBodyWithinBudget`), so a too-large snapshot is never persisted and never authorizes a cutover.

## Deliberately NOT changed: the verifier's decrypt budget

`DEFAULT_MAX_DECRYPT_BYTES` (256 MiB, `agent-backup-verifier.ts`) is left alone on purpose. It is a **per-cycle aggregate** budget spanning a batch of backups, not a per-backup wire size — a different axis. Lowering it to 128 MiB would be a *regression*: one max-size backup would consume an entire cycle, so the sweep would verify a single backup per cycle. At 256 MiB a max-size (128 MiB) backup always fits with room to spare, and `chargeBudget` already distinguishes `payload-exceeds-cycle-budget` (permanent, stop sampling) from `cycle-budget-exhausted` (transient, defer) — so the "can never verify" case is already handled correctly.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix (correctness: removes a retainable-but-unrestorable backup state).

# Documentation changes needed?

My changes do not require a change to the project documentation; the new module documents the contract at its definition.

# Testing

## Where should a reviewer start?

`packages/shared/src/agent-backup-limits.test.ts` — it pins the whole contract: the canonical ceiling is 128 MiB; an override that **lowers** is honored; an override that **raises** (including the exact pre-fix 256 MiB that produced the unrestorable canary snapshot) is clamped; malformed/non-positive fall back; exact-limit passes and limit+1 clamps; and a final invariant case asserting no input can ever resolve a retain budget above the restorable ceiling — the guard that fails if someone raises one side without the other.

# Evidence Details

The load-bearing new property is the **clamp**, not the constant: before this PR an operator could set `ELIZA_SNAPSHOT_MAX_RAW_BYTES=268435456` and silently recreate the exact canary failure. ## Known gaps / failures

Only §1 of #17172 is addressed — §2 (legacy→v2 standby bridge), §3 (additive v2 chunked backup protocol) and §4 (rollout) remain open on the card and are the substantial architecture. This PR makes the current v1 path *safe* (no unrestorable retention) but does not make large agents *backupable* — a >128 MiB agent will now fail cleanly before cutover instead of retaining a dead snapshot, which is the intended §1 behavior ("budget failures are typed, observable, non-retryable, and occur before cutover") and exactly why §3 exists.

[stan-cloud]
a2:Tf77,## What — #17253 §3

**Depends on #17258** (branched on top; the commit beyond it is this PR).

The runner's permanent-failure path settles dependent rows **atomically** — `incrementAttempt(…, onFailedInTx)` flips an APP_DEPLOY's app off `building` in the same transaction as the job's `failed` write. Both **recovery** paths (stale sweep, startup interruption recovery) flipped jobs to `failed` with none of that: `recoverJobFromSnapshot` was a bare update. A recovered-to-failed APP_DEPLOY left its app **`building` forever** — the deploy-status endpoint reports BUILDING indefinitely and every redeploy 409s "A deployment is already in progress" until manual SQL. The code documents this gap itself (the `reEnqueueFailedDeletions` rationale names it verbatim) and explicitly rejects sweeps as the primary signal — so recovery now speaks the runner's own contract instead.

## Design (survived an adversarial plan review: NO-GO as first drafted → GO with 5 amendments, all applied)

- **Same contract, second caller**: `recoverJobFromSnapshot` runs in a transaction, keeps the exact CAS untouched, and invokes the writeback only after the CAS matched — a throw rolls back BOTH writes, mirroring `incrementAttempt` line for line.
- **The landmine the review caught**: writeback builders read payloads **eagerly** and throw on malformed ones — and an offloaded CONTAINER_PROVISION payload keeps `containerId` only in R2. Built inside the transaction, that throw would roll back the flip and wedge the job `in_progress` forever, re-throwing every sweep. The builder therefore runs OUTSIDE the transaction on the **hydrated** job; a build failure degrades to flipping without a writeback, loudly logged.
- **Per-job isolation** in both loops: one poisoned payload rolls back its own job only, never starving the rest of the sweep.
- **No return-shape change**: the recoveries still return a number (~25 call/mock/assertion sites would have broken). Post-commit app-cache eviction rides an optional `onPermanentFailure` hook fed the hydrated failed job; the eviction logic is now one private helper shared with the runner's failure path.
- Recovery has no `UpgradeFailedError`, which lands AGENT_UPGRADE on the **rollback-safe default**: re-armable marker, never `status='error'` on a possibly-live agent.

## Tests

`16 pass / 0 fail` on the rebuilt jobs-recovery harness (hand-rolled DDL replaced with the real drizzle schema via `pushSchema`, apps + its three enums, FK parents seeded, isolated-PGlite loud-skip guard) plus `3 pass` service-side. Verified on the pre-fix code: **4 of the 5 new tests fail** — atomic settle, execution-throw rollback (job back to claimable `in_progress`, app untouched), post-commit hook, stale-path settle. Disclosed: the build-time-throw test pins the *degraded* mode (flip without writeback) and passes on base too, since the old code produced that outcome by accident; it exists to keep the degradation deliberate.

Wiring is tested at the service seam: both recovery paths hand the repository the REAL `buildPermanentFailureWriteback` (produces a closure for APP_DEPLOY, `undefined` for types with no dependent row).

# Risks

Low, and it cannot touch production until an operator runs `install.sh` as root on a runner host. No runtime code changes; the tool itself (`prune-runner-workspaces.ts`, #15504) is unchanged. The scheduled invocation keeps the tool's built-in `Runner.Worker` active-job guard (never passes `--allow-active`), so a timer firing during a live CI job prunes nothing.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

`prune-runner-workspaces.ts` (#15504) is intentionally host-local and documents "run from cron/systemd on the runner host" — but the repo shipped **no timer, cron, or deployment wiring**, so it never ran. That's why prod-2 (`eliza-prod-robot-2`, 98 GB root) refilled to 100% on stale runner `_work` checkouts (51 GB) while Docker cleanup found nothing to reclaim, and an operator cleared it by hand again on 2026-07-15 (per Shaw's triage).

Adds the missing recurring call site as a **system-level systemd bundle** at `packages/deploy/runner-workspace-cleanup/`:

- `units/eliza-runner-workspace-prune.service` — `Type=oneshot`, runs `bun <tool> --root <root> --min-age <hours>`; `ConditionPathExists=<runner root>` makes it a clean no-op on non-runner hosts; `Nice=10` + `IOSchedulingClass=idle` keep it out of the agents' way.
- `units/eliza-runner-workspace-prune.timer` — `OnBootSec=15min`, `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`, `Persistent=false`.
- `install.sh` — idempotent, **root** (the runners' `_work` is under a root-owned `/opt/actions-runners`, unlike the user-level bot bundle in `../systemd/`). Copies the **zero-dependency** tool standalone to `/opt/eliza-runner-workspace-cleanup/`, so the robot needs neither a full checkout nor `node_modules` — only `bun`. Tunables via env (`RUNNER_WORKSPACE_ROOT`, `PRUNE_MIN_AGE_HOURS`, `BUN_BIN`).
- `smoke-test.sh` — static contract check (renders units, asserts no unresolved tokens, asserts the guard is intact and `--allow-active` is absent, asserts a real recurring timer wired to `timers.target`, `bash -n` + `systemd-analyze verify` when available). No root, no install, no host writes.
- `README.md` — operator guide, tunables, verify/uninstall.

## What kind of change is this?

Ops/deployment wiring (no runtime behavior change; fills a missing scheduled call site).

# Documentation changes needed?

The bundle ships its own `README.md`. No other docs change required.

# Testing

## Where should a reviewer start?

`smoke-test.sh` — it encodes the contract: the rendered service invokes the tool with the active-job guard intact (asserts no `--allow-active`), the expected `--root`/`--min-age`, and a real periodic timer bound to `timers.target`. Then `install.sh` (root-only, idempotent, copies the standalone tool + renders units + enables the timer).

## Detailed testing steps

None beyond the static smoke: this is deploy wiring, and the pruning logic is already covered by the tool's own `prune-runner-workspaces.test.ts` (unchanged). Ran locally: `shellcheck` clean, `smoke-test.sh` → `runner-workspace-cleanup smoke OK`. The live ops-apply + two-cycle recurrence proof on the hosts stay with @0xSolace per #15398.

a5:T10fa,## What — the root fix for the #17249 class

**Depends on #17260** (branched on top of it; merge that first — the two commits beyond it are this PR).

`getAgentForLifecycleMutation` was a raw `SELECT * FOR UPDATE`: raw drizzle rows carry timestamptz as **strings** despite the `AgentSandbox` type (drizzle installs identity type parsers and re-maps only typed builders). #17260 fixed the delete crash at two call sites; this types the read itself, healing the whole class.

## What the exhaustive consumer audit found (every date usage classified, ~40 sites)

Three more **live production defects**, invisible to the unit suite because every mock feeds `Date` fixtures:

- **`agent_sleep` was 100% broken** — the commit CAS called `.getTime()` on a raw string (`updated_at` is NOT NULL, so the optional chain never saved it). Every sleep failed at commit; nothing was destroyed, the job just always failed.
- **Managed-launch env updates crashed** — `eq(updated_at, rec.updated_at)` pushed the raw string through the column encoder → `value.toISOString is not a function` → the freshly minted credential was revoked by the compensating teardown.
- **Warm-claimed agents could never complete an upgrade/downgrade** — the in-transaction CAS consults `hasReadyWarmClaimCredential`, whose contract checks `warm_claim_attested_at instanceof Date`; on a raw string that is `false` for every warm-claimed agent → "Agent changed during upgrade", blue torn down, retries exhausted. The same helper answered correctly earlier on the same path from a typed row — two gates silently contradicting each other. **This PR flips that behavior on purpose: warm-claimed upgrades start working.**

## The microsecond trap (why the naive fix was dangerous)

The typed mapping truncates to **milliseconds**; ~20 raw `updated_at = NOW()` writers store **microseconds**. Two exact-equality fences round-tripped the raw string byte-identically and would silently break under typing: the sleep generation CAS and the managed-launch CAS. Both now compare through `date_trunc('milliseconds', column)`. Verified definitively before implementation (adversarial plan review, live probes on V8, JSC, PGlite): JS `Date` parsing **truncates sub-ms lexically, never rounds** — so ms==ms is exact. That invariant is stated in a comment on both fences.

Deliberate residual, documented in code: the five raw `UPDATE … RETURNING *` reads on the warm-claim handoff paths stay raw — the audit traced every consumer and none reads a date field; converting their CASE-heavy SQL to builders is follow-up, not a bundle.

## Tests

`204 pass / 0 fail` across seven suites. New PGlite regressions (raw PGlite rows are strings exactly like production, so the harness is faithful):
- **sleep completes** — fails on base with the exact production error (`getTime is not a function`);
- **sleep CAS survives a µs-precision `updated_at`** — seeded via an explicit SQL literal because PGlite's own `NOW()` is ms-only (a NOW()-seeded row cannot reproduce the mismatch, and the fail-on-base property would be false);
- **the read returns real `Date`s and the warm-claim gate answers `true`** for a ready claimed row — pinning the upgrade-flip mechanically.

Fail-on-base verified: `0 pass / 3 fail` with `getTime is not a function` ×2. One test-only seam change: the warm-claim push suite's fake tx only speaks raw `execute()` SQL, so it now serves the lifecycle read at the helper seam (the same spy every other suite already uses), returning the same mutable row its fake tx keeps updating.

a6:T1928,## The gap (P0, vault audit 2026-07-30, gap #2)

Container provisioning injects caller-supplied `environment_vars` as **plaintext**. Live path, with evidence:

1. `packages/cloud/services/container-control-plane/src/index.ts:1181` — `POST /api/v1/containers` → `toCreateInput()` (`:509 environmentVars: asRecordOfStrings(body.environment_vars)`) and `PATCH :1246` → `client.setEnv(...)`. This sidecar is the production executor: Worker routes forward here because Workers can't SSH (README; `packages/cloud/api/v1/_container-control-plane-forward.ts`).
2. `packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/containers/hetzner-client/client.ts` — `createContainer` persists `environment_vars` into the DB row (`:118`) and builds `docker create -e KEY=value` flags shipped over SSH (`:256-258`); `setEnv` repeats both (`:650, :681`).

So each secret lands in: the `containers.environment_vars` jsonb, the SSH command line (node shell history / logs), and `docker inspect` on the shared node.

## The fix

New `CONTAINERS_ENV_VAULT_REFS` flag (**default OFF**). When on, `createContainer`/`setEnv` seal secret-bearing values (same `isSensitiveAgentEnvKey` heuristic as the #11332 at-rest crypto; reserved platform keys and non-secret config untouched) into the Steward secret vault (`POST /secrets`, 409 → versioned rotate via `PUT /secrets/:id`) **before** any DB or SSH side effect. The container env then carries only `vault://<key>` sentinels using the exact format owned by `packages/agent/src/runtime/operations/vault-bridge.ts` (`resolveConfigEnvForProcess` — no new scheme invented; boot-side resolution is a sibling lane).

- **Fail closed:** vault outage aborts the provision; no silent plaintext fallback.
- **Idempotent:** values already carrying refs are not re-sealed; recreate/setEnv rotates the same project-scoped secret rows (`cloud/env/<org>/<project>/<KEY>`) — no orphans.
- **Backward compatible:** flag off = byte-for-byte legacy behavior (proven by test). Migration: configure `STEWARD_API_URL` + `STEWARD_TENANT_API_KEY`/`STEWARD_TENANT_ID` on the control-plane sidecar, flip the flag, recreate containers (env is create-time-only in Docker anyway).

## Tests (bidirectional proof)

`env-vault-refs.test.ts` (unit): ref-format parity with vault-bridge, secret/non-secret partitioning, 409→rotate, fail-closed on create and rotate failures.

`client.env-vault-refs.test.ts` (live-path integration, same harness pattern as `client.error-policy.test.ts`):
- flag ON → the **actual** `docker create` command line and persisted row contain no secret values, only `vault://` refs; the in-memory steward holds the values; non-secret `NODE_ENV` still injected plainly.
- flag ON + steward down → provision throws `container_create_failed` with **zero** DB/SSH side effects.
- flag OFF → `docker create` carries the raw value, row is plaintext, zero vault traffic (legacy unchanged).

17/17 pass locally (incl. the pre-existing error-policy suite); `tsc --noEmit` clean; biome clean.

Receipt: `projects/steward/CLOUD-ENV-PLAINTEXT-2026-07-30.md` (workspace).

Extracted from #17206. Credit to @lalalune for the original replay analysis and to @0xSolace for isolating the production approval path.

## Root cause

`RESOLVE_REQUEST` used plugin-local error classes while the live `ApprovalService` throws the distinct classes exported by `@elizaos/agent`. Duplicate or concurrent decisions could therefore escape as uncaught errors. More importantly, treating `approved` as completed could suppress execution after a crash before dispatch, while retrying an `executing` row could duplicate an external side effect after a crash following dispatch.

## Repair

- import and recognize the exact error constructors from both queue implementations; forged lookalike errors still propagate
- require `byId` and the execution-transition methods before any decision mutation
- treat `approved` as a durable outbox row that can be claimed after a pre-dispatch crash
- use `markExecuting` as the atomic at-most-once dispatch claim
- treat only `done` as completed success
- surface `executing` as `APPROVAL_EXECUTION_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` and never retry it blindly
- re-read after compare-and-swap races so approve/approve and approve/reject races preserve the single winning decision

This deliberately guarantees durable at-most-once dispatch, not exactly-once completion. Connector APIs do not expose a universal idempotency/reconciliation key; a crash after the execution claim may therefore require provider or owner reconciliation.

## Validation

- exact head: `8aff20d01a65661f09318aa1104bb9fdddc37e56`
- exact base: `00d6f6cdaeb40d9d70e9664ebaccbd8169718f26`
- real agent-side approval store on PGlite, including crash recovery and forced races: 14/14 passed
- focused executor tests: 14/14 passed
- focused Biome and `git diff --check`: passed
- exact-head CI and independent re-review: pending

ae:T186d,## What — #17253 §3

**Supersedes #17263.** That PR was branched on top of the rejected #17258, so its diff still carried the interruption-counter design you turned down. This is a clean re-cut on current `develop`: writeback only, no counter, none of the #17258 commits. The durable counter is a separate lot and will land on its own once this is in.

The live execution path already settles a job's dependent status row atomically with its permanent-failure flip — `incrementAttempt(…, onFailedInTx)` flips an APP_DEPLOY's app off `building` in the same transaction as the job's `failed` write. The recovery sweeps did not: `recoverJobFromSnapshot` was a bare update, so a recovered-to-failed APP_DEPLOY left its app `building` and every redeploy 409'd until manual SQL. The code names this gap itself (the `reEnqueueFailedDeletions` rationale) and explicitly rejects sweeps as the primary signal. Recovery now speaks the same contract.

## Design

- **Same contract, second caller.** The writeback runs inside the recovery transaction, only after the CAS matched. A throw rolls back the flip and the dependent write together, so the next sweep retries the pair rather than leaving half a state change behind. The CAS itself is untouched.
- **Hydration stays outside the transaction.** Builders read payloads eagerly and an offloaded CONTAINER_PROVISION payload keeps `containerId` only in the blob store, which has no timeout — and the transaction holds the agent-lifecycle advisory lock. So the builder runs on the hydrated job, before the transaction opens.
- **The value the writeback receives equals `hydrateJob(updated)` exactly**, rebuilt with no in-transaction blob read: recovery never touches `data`/`result`, so the pre-transaction hydration of those two is byte-identical, and the fresh `error` is the plaintext just written. That same value is what `recoverJobFromSnapshot` returns, so the post-commit cache eviction sees what the live path sees.
- **Per-job isolation, outage still audible.** One poisoned payload rolls back its own job only. A batch where *every* job failed throws — that is an infrastructure outage and the caller alerts on it.
- **Fail-closed, like the live path.** A writeback that cannot be built leaves the job `in_progress` for the next sweep. Flipping it without settling its dependent row is the exact half-state this change exists to remove, so there is no degrade branch.
- **Recovery asks per job TYPE whether a dependent row exists**, before it hydrates anything. Types that own none get no builder and pay no object-store reads — which also keeps true the invariant that lets the stale sweep skip lane filtering (flipping a stuck row back to `pending` stays DB-only). The type list and the switch arms are one mapping; the switch fails to compile if they drift.
- **The apps daemon got the process boundary it was missing.** Startup recovery was called with no handler, so an all-failed batch — routinely one row on a lane that small — exited the process, systemd restarted into the same row, and the lane claimed nothing. Its sibling worker already wraps the same sweep.

Recovery has no `UpgradeFailedError`, which lands AGENT_UPGRADE on the rollback-safe default: re-armable marker, never `status='error'` on a possibly-live agent.

## What changed since #17263, beyond dropping the counter

The first cut of this work had four defects of its own, found by adversarially verifying it rather than trusting the green suite:

1. The post-commit hook was handed the **raw** row while the in-transaction writeback got the hydrated one. Production offloads payloads, so `readContainerProvisionJobData` threw on every offloaded job and was swallowed by its own J7 warn — the deploy-status route kept reporting `building` for the full cache TTL, precisely the failure that hook exists to prevent.
2. The hydration guard **degraded open**: an unreachable blob store meant the job still flipped to `failed` with its dependent row untouched, and because the degrade sat one frame below the per-job catch it never counted toward the all-failed signal, so the sweep returned a healthy-looking number.
3. Resolving a writeback hydrated **every** job type, including lanes deliberately left gated, falsifying the in-repo comment that justifies not lane-filtering the stale sweep.
4. The apps daemon crash loop above.

## Tests

`18 pass / 0 fail` on the recovery harness, `16 pass` on the service writeback seams, `208 pass` on the canary diagnostic sanitizer, `6 pass` on the apps worker.

The offloaded path is now driven for real against an in-memory bucket — every previous fixture was `inline`, which is exactly what made defect 1 invisible. Reverting the hydrated return turns that test red. The test that could not fail (it passed on base too) was replaced by one proving the fail-closed behavior.

The full `src/db/repositories` batch run shows 11 failures **on `develop` as well** — pre-existing cross-file pollution in batch mode, unrelated to this diff; the same run adds 6 passing tests and no new failures.

The canary diagnostic stops refusing recovery-authored terminal failures as permanent-delete envelope sources, since recovery is now a legitimate writer of them. No fence was weakened: job-level validation already pins a terminal message's own attempt count to the job's `attempts` and `max_attempts`, which the correlation equalities pin to the envelope's.

# Risks

Low and tightly bounded. This changes only the read-only admin diagnostic sanitizer and its tests. It does not alter production deletion, retry, recovery, SQL, workflow permissions, deployments, devices, or staging state.

The raw permanent-delete cause is used only for an in-memory exact-equality join against the already bounded newest-three jobs. It is never normalized, hashed, profiled again, emitted, logged, or written. Schema version 3 and its output keys are unchanged.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

The first post-#17198 read-only run correctly stopped at `agent.errorMessage`: the sandbox row retains the canonical permanent-delete wrapper while recovery may add newer delete jobs. A coarse code or profile match would be ambiguous and could expand the disclosure surface.

This PR:

- parses exactly one bounded canonical permanent-delete envelope;
- binds its attempt counter and raw cause to an exact exhausted failed job in the already bounded history;
- reuses that job's existing sanitized error code instead of emitting a second profile or source index;
- requires deletion ownership and a positive persisted failure count;
- requires `deletion_failed` to bind job zero;
- permits `deletion_pending` to cross only the producer-proven recovery chain: an optional sole active job at index zero plus strict terminal timeout/worker-restart recovery records;
- rejects unrelated intermediaries, strict terminal records masquerading as the source, exhausted/completed/unstarted active retries, malformed/nested/case/punctuation envelope lookalikes, raw mismatches, and lifecycle/counter contradictions;
- preserves fail-closed no-artifact behavior.

No raw, normalized, hashed, substring-derived, or position-derived cause material enters canonical output.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix for a read-only operational diagnostic.

# Documentation changes needed?

No project documentation change is required. The fixed schema, source-correlation boundary, recovery ordering, and privacy invariants are executable contracts in the sanitizer tests.

A narrow extraction of the deterministic owner-local time resolver from @lalalune's draft #17206, rebased onto current `develop` (`27d21400c9a`).

After Shaw's blocking reviews, this PR is now **DST resolver work only**. It contains no calendar availability/source-health API, no `DispatchReceipt`, and no reservation metadata helper.

## What lands

- One canonical `HH:MM` → UTC resolver shared by due evaluation, next-fire indexing, and the production/fallback anchor registries.
- Temporal-compatible DST behavior:
  - ambiguous fall-back times choose the earlier occurrence;
  - skipped local times advance by the timezone gap;
  - non-hour transitions are supported;
  - a whole skipped local date advances by the date-line gap.
- `InvalidLocalTimeError` distinguishes malformed supplied values from genuinely absent owner facts.
  - Missing values may still use an intentional default.
  - Malformed values never become `null`, never silently select a default, and produce the same typed failure in due and index paths.

## Boundary coverage

- America/New_York spring/fall transitions
- Europe/Berlin spring/fall transitions
- Australia/Lord_Howe 30-minute transitions
- **America/Santiago 2026-09-06**, where local midnight does not exist and `00:00` resolves compatibly to `01:00`
- **Pacific/Apia 2011-12-30**, where the entire local date was skipped
- The registered production anchor path, not only the `anchors: null` fallback path

The earlier availability/source-health evaluator, `DispatchReceipt` additions, and reservation helper have been removed completely.

Availability can return only with authoritative per-grant acquisition, pagination/coverage proof, canonical sync/tombstone identity, and sanitized public failures. Receipt types can return only with enforcement in runner policy, persistence, and real connector paths.

## Root cause

Two develop failures were opaque rather than product failures:

- Bun completed the full `packages/scripts` sweep with 1,236 tests and 24,494 assertions, but its valid CI `<properties>` metadata was rejected by the strict JUnit parser. The runner then collapsed the Bun child exit and evidence-validation exit into one code.
- Windows grouped multiple typechecks/builds into concurrent Turbo processes, hiding the failing package and triggering `STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED` under resource pressure. The scheduled-backup PGlite fixture also used drizzle-kit `pushSchema`, whose internal `process.exit(1)` could terminate the entire multi-file runner.

## Repair

- accept Bun’s exact `properties/property` JUnit shape while rejecting duplicate, nested, attributed, textual, or testcase-smuggling metadata
- record child and evidence exit codes independently and derive the final exit without losing either cause
- run Windows typechecks per package for attribution
- prove `plugin-coding-tools` independently, then run the remaining Turbo build graph serially
- use shared plain PGlite DDL for scheduled-backup coverage
- make Miniflare build filters separator-portable and sibling-safe

# Background

## What does this PR do?

The staging canary diagnostic correctly stopped when the newest delete job contained an error not covered by its privacy-safe classifier. This PR adds a deliberately coarse `unclassified` profile for that one field only:

- known classifiers still run first;
- only `jobs[0].error` may use the fallback;
- no raw text, normalized text, hash, substring, identifier, or secret is emitted;
- output contains only a bounded length bucket and one-hot-or-none fixed writer hints;
- malformed recovery, sandbox errors, `result.error`, and older job errors still fail closed;
- impossible job/status/result combinations still fail closed.

The workflow and SQL query are byte-identical to the base.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix (non-breaking diagnostic observability fix).

b5:T12aa,Closes #17428.

## What changed

- removes the route-level chat generation deadline and both branded timeout environment aliases
- removes the independent `MessageService` deadline so one turn has one owner
- propagates caller cancellation through a single `AbortSignal` to document augmentation, model generation, planner execution, and streaming
- disables Node's whole-request and idle-socket deadlines for streaming chat while retaining bounded header and keep-alive handling
- makes ingress trajectory-hook failure reject before generation instead of returning an answer whose ingress record is missing
- makes conversation-title generation follow the caller lifecycle instead of an unrelated 5 second timer
- preserves the training roleplay API's explicit timeout option by expressing it as caller-owned `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`

## Why

A fixed response deadline cannot distinguish a dead request from a healthy long generation. Racing a timeout against generation can return an error while model/tool work, persistence, and callbacks continue in the background. The request/disconnect owner now controls cancellation, and downstream work receives that same signal.

Replaces closed composite PR #16269 with only the package-launcher verification contract. Store screenshot and unrelated packaging metadata changes are deliberately excluded.

## Problem

Five Snap, Debian, and Flatpak smoke steps converted failed `--version` or `--help` commands into green diagnostics. A package with a missing runtime dependency, wrong version, empty help, or a hanging launcher could therefore proceed to publication.

## Change

- Add one bounded process verifier for exact version plus populated Commander help.
- Use it in all Snap, Debian, and Flatpak smoke steps before publication or artifact attachment.
- Hard-kill commands that exceed the timeout and cap captured output.
- Cover startup failure, dependency failure, version mismatch, malformed help, hangs, wrapper arguments, CLI exit behavior, workflow masking, and publication order with real Node child processes and parsed workflow YAML.

b9:Tb4e,Fixes #17521.

## What changed

- runs every `Quality (Fork)` lane on `ubuntu-24.04`, removing persistent workspace and runner-service state from untrusted fork validation
- pins the fork lane to the canonical released CI Bun version (`1.3.14`)
- isolates setup-bun's Unix `HOME` and Windows `USERPROFILE` by run, attempt, job, and matrix entry in the shared workspace action, cloud setup action, and direct CLI lane
- disables setup-bun's executable cache for those ephemeral paths, preventing per-run cache-version churn while preserving package and Turbo caches
- separates manual exact-head dispatch concurrency from pull-request metadata runs so skipped PR jobs cannot cancel queued proof
- enforces hosted selection for every current and future fork job, derives the Bun pin from `.github/ci-bun-version.json`, binds isolated homes to parsed setup-bun steps, and rejects same-repository pull requests through mutation tests

## Why

Quality (Fork) run 30688698836 assigned Build and CLI smoke to two registrations on the same Hetzner host. Both were canceled inside actions/checkout while `git clean -ffdx` was running; no setup or repository command executed. GitHub's recorded job completion timestamps precede the checkout logs, and the same registrations have produced prior canceled jobs after successful commands. Hosted runners provide a fresh workspace and process boundary for this security-sensitive fork lane.

## What changed

- starts independent FACTS history/identity reads together, then all fact candidate pools together
- batches RELATIONSHIPS counterpart lookup into one adapter query
- preserves WORLD's authoritative world dependency, then overlaps room and participant reads
- overlaps DOCUMENTS search and inventory while coalescing their immutable requester authorization per turn
- preserves document tenant isolation in the unscoped mutation existence probe
- converts FACTS database failure from fabricated healthy-empty context into a typed `ElizaError`
- hardens the all-provider telemetry report: invalid sample settings fail, values use stable precision, and fresh vs maximum-reuse behavior is verified structurally without latency thresholds

## Critical scope decisions

This does not start WORLD-dependent reads before the world exists, and it does not remove or reassign relationship components. Those are semantic changes, not latency refactors. It also does not add response timeouts or numeric CI ratchets.

bb:Tb24,# Overall Project Weekly Summary (Jul 26 - 1, 2026)

## Executive Summary
This week, the ElizaOS team focused on hardening our core infrastructure to ensure a stable, reliable foundation for our growing agent ecosystem. By resolving critical production issues and streamlining our development processes, we have improved the framework's resilience while making significant progress on the new "Agentic Parent Suite" for household coordination.

### Key Strategic Initiatives & Outcomes

**Strengthening Platform Reliability**
_Goal: We aimed to eliminate production errors and ensure that our agents operate consistently and predictably._
- Resolved critical failures in agent management, ensuring that agents can be created and removed without system errors ([elizaos/eliza](https://github.com/elizaos/eliza/pull/17260)).
- Improved the accuracy of agent monitoring and data tracking, ensuring that user interactions and wallet balances are recorded correctly ([elizaos/eliza](https://github.com/elizaos/eliza/pull/17140)).
- Optimized our internal testing and deployment pipelines to prevent system crashes and speed up development workflows ([elizaos/eliza](https://github.com/elizaos/eliza/pull/17238)).

**Expanding Agent Capabilities**
_Goal: We are building new features that allow agents to handle complex, real-world tasks like household management and on-chain execution._
- Advanced the "Agentic Parent Suite," a new initiative designed to help agents manage household schedules and coordination ([elizaos/eliza](https://github.com/elizaos/eliza/issues/17175)).
- Began integrating the Aomi plugin, which will enable agents to perform more sophisticated on-chain executions ([elizaos/eliza](https://github.com/elizaos/eliza/issues/17288)).

c5:T190f,## Goal

Ship a trustworthy LifeOps parent-assistant suite that materially reduces the
anticipation, planning, coordination, monitoring, and recovery work carried by
a busy world-traveling mother coordinating children with a co-parent and
caregivers.

The completed system must ingest authoritative household sources, reason over
multiple calendars without leaking private event details, distinguish proposals
from agreements, obtain the right approvals, monitor material changes, execute
typed transactions exactly once, and verify closure. It must expose source
freshness and errors instead of presenting unavailable data as a healthy empty
state.

## Design doc

`packages/docs/ongoing-development/research/11-agentic-parent-suite.md`

## Scope

- Calendar source registry, sync health, multi-account aggregation, guest
  free/busy, ICS/webcal, and Microsoft Graph calendar support.
- Deterministic conflict/availability evaluation for time, people, custody,
  caregivers, transport, locations, resources, travel, recurrence, time zones,
  DST, and all-day events.
- Typed schedule proposals, per-party agreements, material-change
  invalidation, approval-gated messaging, and provider materialization.
- Household roles, scoped/expiring caregiver access, private-busy projection,
  append-only audit, and scoped export.
- School/activity ingestion and correction monitoring; action bundles,
  responsibility ownership, seasonal opportunities, household items, and
  external-source adapters.
- Food constraints, inventory confidence, cart/order idempotency, delivery
  exception recovery, childcare/work modeling, and source-grounded parenting
  guidance with human handoff.
- A composite world-traveling co-parent persona plus G1-G48 capability
  scenarios, real-provider tests, live-model trajectories, and manually
  reviewed evidence.

## Non-goals

- A second scheduler, household graph, connector abstraction, or file store.
- Behavior keyed from prompt text or demographic runtime modes.
- Autonomous sensitive messages, custody changes, medical/legal decisions, or
  purchases without typed policy and required approval.
- Scraping private guest calendars or fabricating availability, inventory,
  costs, source health, transactions, or completion.

## Work Items

- [ ] Ratify calendar-source health, proposal/agreement, access, audit,
      responsibility, provenance, and transaction contracts.
- [ ] Consolidate conflict detection and wire production guest free/busy.
- [ ] Route scheduling lifecycle communication through draft and approval
      policy.
- [ ] Implement provider-neutral sync, pagination, cursors, webhooks, and
      idempotent reconciliation.
- [ ] Implement Microsoft and hardened ICS/webcal sources.
- [ ] Implement household roles, scoped access, private-busy, audit, and export.
- [ ] Implement schedule proposals, approvals, materiality, and final
      calendar materialization.
- [ ] Implement school/activity ingestion, correction monitoring, action
      bundles, and weekly responsibility review.
- [ ] Implement weather/maps/local-activity sources and seasonal/household
      item workflows.
- [ ] Implement food, inventory, cart, order, refund, and delivery-recovery
      workflows.
- [ ] Implement deterministic childcare/work scenarios and source-grounded
      parenting guidance boundaries.
- [ ] Author and live-verify G1-G48 plus all ten Jordan co-parent scenarios.
- [ ] Reconcile every overlapping open LifeOps issue and PR; reuse valid work
      and close no item until the production path and evidence are complete.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every row in the design doc delivery ledger is complete.
- [ ] The busy world-traveling co-parent journey works from source ingestion
      through conflict discovery, privacy-preserving coordination, approval,
      materialization, change recovery, and closure.
- [ ] Loading, designed-empty, unavailable, stale, partial, and error states are
      distinguishable at every source boundary.
- [ ] No private event title, child-private fact, or unrelated adult data leaks
      across household scopes or exports.
- [ ] Duplicate/out-of-order provider events, retries, concurrent approvals,
      recurrence edits, DST/date-line crossings, and transaction retries are
      deterministic and idempotent.
- [ ] Real-provider or sandbox-provider contracts cover every connector; mocks
      and deterministic LLM fixtures are supplemental only.
- [ ] Live-model scenarios record inputs, provider context, actions, outputs,
      and domain artifacts, and every artifact is manually reviewed.
- [ ] Full package tests, repository verification, and all applicable UI,
      security, and evidence gates pass after rebasing on `origin/develop`.

c6:T1200,## Summary

A live production audit of the provisioning pipeline (2026-07-29) found **agent deletion is failing 100% of the time**, and has been for days. This is customer-visible and accelerating.

Over the last 7 days: **554 failed jobs vs 153 completed** (78% failure rate).

## 1. `agent_delete` is completely broken — 160/160 failures, one identical cause

Every failed `agent_delete` job in the window carries the same error:

```
value.toISOString is not a function
```

- 160 failures, all identical, most recent **2026-07-28 18:03 UTC** (still current).
- All of them exhausted `attempts >= max_attempts` — so each one also burned the full retry budget.
- Consequence: **37 agents are stuck in `deletion_failed`**, up from 5 five days ago, and accelerating: **17 of them in the last 24 hours alone**.
- Customers who ask to delete an agent get a failure, the agent stays, and it keeps occupying node capacity.

`value.toISOString is not a function` is Drizzle's timestamp serializer receiving a **string where a `Date` is expected** — the same class as the cache/JSON round-trip defect fixed in #16859/#16860 for `resolveSharedAgent`.

One concrete candidate worth checking first (not yet proven to be the site): `prepareAgentBackupInsertData` (`packages/cloud/shared/src/db/repositories/agent-sandboxes.ts`) does

```ts
const createdAt = data.created_at ?? new Date();
// ...
created_at: createdAt,
```

`??` only guards `null`/`undefined` — a value that already crossed a JSON boundary as an ISO **string** passes straight through into the timestamp column. The 4 non-restart `agent_snapshot` failures in the same window are literally `Failed query: insert into "agent_sandbox_backups" (...)`, which is that insert.

## 2. `agent_snapshot`: 386 failures, 381 of them not the job's fault

```
Job interrupted by worker restart 2 times - max attempts reached   (381)
Failed query: insert into "agent_sandbox_backups" ...              (4)
Job timed out 2 times - max attempts reached                       (1)
```

The worker keeps restarting mid-snapshot, and **each restart consumes an attempt**. Two restarts exhaust `max_attempts` and the job is marked permanently failed — even though nothing about the job itself failed. A restart is an infrastructure event, not a job defect, and should not spend the job's retry budget (the codebase already has the shape for this: `retryLaterWithoutIncrementingAttempts`).

Why the worker restarts so often is the second half of this: it is consistent with the heap abort in #17154 and with the unbounded source-side snapshot capture in #17172 §1 (a large agent's capture is materialized entirely in the worker's heap).

## 3. The fleet is at or over capacity

| node | capacity | running |
|---|---|---|
| eliza-core-prod-2 | 24 | 24 |
| eliza-core-prod-3 | 24 | **25** |
| eliza-core-prod-4 | 24 | 24 |
| eliza-core-prod-5 | 24 | 24 |
| eliza-core-prod-6 | 24 | 24 |

prod-3 is **over** its declared capacity, and every robot is full, so new work is spilling onto autoscaled cloud nodes (3 × 4 running). Note the interaction: the 37 undeletable agents and the 45 in `error` are holding slots that should have been reclaimed — the delete failure is directly feeding the capacity pressure.

Also present: a `knowledge_processing` job stuck `in_progress` since **2025-12-31** (~7 months), which no sweeper has reclaimed.

## Why these compound

The three interact rather than being independent:
1. Deletes fail → agents accumulate (`deletion_failed` 37, `error` 45) → capacity fills.
2. Snapshots fail on worker restart → upgrades/deletes that depend on a restore point are less safe.
3. Full capacity → more scheduling pressure → longer boots → more exposure to the sweeper/timeout classes (#17215).

## Asks

- [ ] Pin and fix the `toISOString` write in the delete path — deterministic, 100% reproducible, highest customer impact.
- [ ] A worker restart must not consume a job's retry budget (`retryLaterWithoutIncrementingAttempts` semantics for interruption).
- [ ] Recover the 37 `deletion_failed` + 45 `error` rows once the above land (see #17162 for the 44-agent precedent and its recovery constraints).
- [ ] Reconcile declared capacity vs actual (prod-3 at 25/24), and reclaim the 7-month-stuck `in_progress` job.

Evidence gathered live against production (counts, error strings, timings; no customer identifiers). Related: #17215 (sweeper vs in-flight cold boots), #17154 (worker heap abort), #17172 (snapshot budgets), #17162 (the 2026-07-13 stranding), #17185 (delete must release capacity exactly once). ## Scope

Launch `eliza.computer` from this monorepo as a minimal Vite site that turns spare agent compute into reviewable elizaOS contributions. Ship a downloadable/runnable skill that selects and finishes issues, reviews open PRs, adds missing tests/evidence/validation/screenshots/video, follows the repository claim and evidence workflow, and discloses the exact model used. Add a transparent GitHub-backed contribution leaderboard, Cloudflare Pages CI/CD, and the contribution/template changes needed to make model attribution durable.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A bundled, validated, installable contribution skill handles issue-finishing and PR-review workflows safely.
- [ ] The skill enforces claims, sync/rebase, package guidance, scoped validation, real evidence, independent review, and model disclosure.
- [ ] A responsive, accessible Vite site explains the workflow, installs/downloads the skill, surfaces open work, and renders a transparent elizaOS/eliza leaderboard.
- [ ] Leaderboard scoring covers merged PRs, issue work, substantive comments/reviews, evidence, and model disclosure with anti-gaming caps and documented methodology.
- [ ] PR/issue contribution guidance records model provenance, including a human-only declaration path.
- [ ] Unit, integration, build, accessibility, responsive, and real browser E2E checks pass; desktop/mobile screenshots and an MP4 walkthrough are manually reviewed.
- [ ] Cloudflare Pages deployment and custom domain are configured and production is verified over HTTPS.

Related: #17426.cd:T933,## Root cause (proven side-by-side)

`.github/workflows/cloud-tests.yml` (and sibling workflows) select runners with:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ fromJSON(vars.HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE == 'false' && '["ubuntu-24.04"]' || '["self-hosted","hetzner-robot"]') }}
```

The repo variable `HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE` has been **`false` since 2026-07-05**. But **configuration variables are not delivered to workflow runs for pull requests from forks** — `vars.HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE` evaluates as empty there, `'' == 'false'` is false, and the expression falls through to the fleet branch.

Observed at 2026-07-31 ~09:30Z, same workflow file, same commit window:

| PR | head repo | cloud lanes ran on |
|---|---|---|
| #17435 (same-repo branch) | elizaOS/eliza | `ubuntu-24.04` (GitHub-hosted) — [run 30620004875](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/30620004875) |
| #17349 (fork) | standujar/eliza | `self-hosted, hetzner-robot` — [run 30617154040](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/30617154040): eliza-prod-robot-5-r3, eliza-prod-robot-2-r1, eliza-prod-robot-4-r3, eliza-prod-robot-3-r2 |

## Impact

Every **fork** PR — i.e. the entire standujar/0xSolace swarm output — has its cloud lanes (and the other ~40 workflows using this expression) routed onto the offline, degraded fleet: docker.sock permission failures (prod-robot-2, prod-robot-5), `_diag/pages` corruption (robots 10/12/19/20), I/O starvation (10-min cache-key computations), ETXTBSY bun races, and round-number timeout kills. Full receipts in #17421. Same-repo PRs sail through on GitHub-hosted runners. This asymmetry is why the fork-PR queue has been stuck in rerun roulette all morning.

## Fix (one mechanical expression change, repo-wide)

Make the gate **fail-safe** for a missing variable — route to GitHub-hosted unless the fleet is explicitly online:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ fromJSON(vars.HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE != 'true' && '["ubuntu-24.04"]' || '["self-hosted","hetzner-robot"]') }}
```

`grep -rl "HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE == 'false'" .github/workflows/ | xargs sed -i "s/HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE == 'false'/HETZNER_FLEET_ONLINE != 'true'/g"` — then flip the variable to `true` only when the fleet is actually healthy.

Claimed by: shaw-codexd2:T1807,## Problem

The production admin-canary upgrade for the demo agent failed safely before cutover because the mandatory pre-upgrade snapshot exceeded the Cloud raw hydration budget:

- production deploy: `main@054fc9feff4f95dc97409cc7b703e2e45600ebcc`
- canary workflow: `30183809168`
- canary job: `771bc989-3244-41d7-bb03-c9ff565be8c6`
- sanitized actor-bound cause: `Pre-upgrade snapshot failed: Snapshot payload exceeds the raw hydration budget (268435456 bytes) — refusing to retain it`

The current v1 agent snapshot eagerly materializes one JSON document containing every agent-owned shared-Postgres row, including derived embeddings, plus base64 local files. Cloud accepts up to 256 MiB, while `/api/restore` and backup-chain reconstruction cap at 128 MiB, so a 128–256 MiB snapshot can authorize a cutover but be impossible to restore. R2 offload happens only after the whole payload has already been downloaded, parsed, reserialized, encrypted, and retained.

For managed Cloud agents, old and new containers use the same external Postgres database. Copying that database into the container snapshot is both wasteful and semantically dangerous: the current rollback restore deletes/reinserts live shared rows while the current image may still be serving.

This extends #16639; it is the rollout-blocking correctness closure discovered by the exact production canary.

## Required architecture

### 1. Immediate v1 safety alignment

- Define one canonical v1 maximum restorable wire size shared by agent restore, Cloud fetch, backup reconstruction, and verification; it must not exceed 128 MiB.
- Add source-side aggregate/raw/expanded budgeting so the agent aborts before eagerly retaining every component.
- Budget failures are typed, observable, privacy-safe, non-retryable, and occur before cutover.
- Keep manual/auto v1 behavior for genuinely small backups; do not raise heap or body limits.

### 2. Legacy-to-v2 standby bridge

The first rollout crosses an image-protocol boundary: the old image emits only v1 and rejects a v2 database reference. A projected v1 payload cannot make old restore safe because an empty/partial `postgres-rows` restore deletes data.

- Add a distinct durable legacy-standby lifecycle; do not reuse `replacement_cleanup_*`, whose reconciler semantics mean “garbage to destroy.”
- After the new image is provisioned and healthy, stop-preserve the exact old container, volume, VPN identity, image digest, environment generation, and capacity ownership.
- Atomically cut traffic to the new placement while retaining the old stopped container as rollback authority.
- Any failed acceptance CAS-switches back to that exact standby without calling old `/api/restore`.
- Standby retirement requires a verified v2 restore point and explicit acceptance; time alone may never retire it.
- Recovery/reconciliation must be crash-safe and generation/CAS fenced.

### 3. Additive v2 backup protocol

- `POST /api/snapshot` accepts a bounded purpose/capability contract.
- Shared/BYO Postgres is represented by a credential-free, agent-bound connection-identity fingerprint/reference; restore requires an exact match and performs zero SQL deletes/inserts.
- PGlite remains a real captured/restored database component.
- Local media, vault, character/config, and state are streamed as deterministic bounded archive chunks.
- Reuse `agent_sandbox_backups` and the existing tenant-scoped backup namespace. Store an encrypted descriptor plus chunk objects; do not introduce a second backup store.
- Each fixed-size chunk uses authenticated encryption with AAD binding organization, sandbox, backup, schema, index, and size. Hashes/nonces/tags live in the descriptor; commit the descriptor only after every chunk verifies.
- Restore streams, decrypts, verifies, and stages all components before destructive apply. Reject traversal, symlinks, malformed/truncated streams, wrong tenant/agent/database identity, and partial data.
- Reconcile the required R2 bindings into the provisioning daemon. Existing whole-string object helpers must not carry v2.

### 4. Rollout

- Prefer a narrow bridge image first, then the feature image, so rollback-protocol risk is isolated.
- The first legacy→v2 canary retains the old standby through real v2 restore proof.
- After the v2 image becomes the declared rollback floor, subsequent blue/green upgrades use v2 backups and the ordinary cleanup path.
- Never bypass the mandatory restore point, silently drop local state, or treat the external-Postgres reference as a disaster backup.

## Acceptance and evidence

- [ ] Exact-limit v1 passes; limit+1 fails before cutover; Cloud and restore limits cannot diverge.
- [ ] Source-side snapshot collection stays bounded and cancels promptly.
- [ ] A >256 MiB legacy fixture crosses the protocol boundary with bounded worker memory while the old standby remains rollback-capable.
- [ ] Crash/retry at every standby phase converges exactly once without destroying the serving or rollback placement.
- [ ] Failed acceptance CAS-restores the exact old standby without `/api/restore`.
- [ ] v2 shared-Postgres restore validates identity, issues zero SQL, and preserves rows written after snapshot.
- [ ] PGlite, media, vault, character/config, and state round-trip exactly, including corrupt/truncated/adversarial cases.
