The bundle-aware Cloud release audit merged in #17067 is package-independent only for the four LP3 classes. Ordinary entries in `ANDROID_CLOUD_STRIPPED_COMPONENTS` are compared after qualification against the application ID, and forbidden permissions are collected only from `<uses-permission*>` elements.

A dynamic-feature/library manifest can therefore relocate a forbidden repo-owned service and carry its privileged binding on the component itself, for example:

```xml
<service
  android:name="com.feature.ElizaAccessibilityService"
  android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE" />
```

That component is not application-ID-qualified, is not one of the LP3-only suffix checks, and its `android:permission` is not inspected. The matching non-LP3 class is also absent from the package-independent DEX scan. A release AAB can therefore pass while retaining a Cloud/Play-forbidden privileged service in a feature module.

d6:Tf05,## Summary

`markStuckProvisioningWithoutActiveJobAsError` exempts only two job types, but **four** job types legitimately hold a row in `provisioning`. A `agent_wake` or `agent_resume` that takes longer than 10 minutes — while still well inside its **own 15-minute cold-boot budget** — has its sandbox flipped to terminal `error` mid-flight, and the container can then be reaped out from under the still-running job.

This is not hypothetical. It is the mechanism behind **19 of the 44 agents stranded on 2026-07-13** (RCA in #17162): those 19 carry exactly the message this predicate writes.

## The defect

`packages/cloud/shared/src/db/repositories/agent-sandboxes.ts:747` writes:

> `Agent was stuck in provisioning state with no active provisioning job.`

and 13 lines below, `:760`, decides who is exempt:

```sql
AND ${jobs.type} IN ('agent_provision', 'agent_restart')
```

The same two-type predicate appears three times in that file (`:360`, `:760`, `:1040`).

But `provisioning` is also owned by wake and resume:

- `eliza-sandbox.ts` `executeResume` → `this.provision(...)`
- `eliza-sandbox.ts` `executeWake` → `this.provision(...)` (two call sites)

and `provision()` takes the row to `status: 'provisioning'` via `trySetProvisioning`.

Both types are declared **cold boot** with a 15-minute budget (`provisioning-jobs.ts`: `AGENT_RESUME` / `AGENT_WAKE` in `COLD_BOOT_JOB_TYPES`, `COLD_BOOT_STALE_JOB_THRESHOLD_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000`), while the sweeper cutoff is **10 minutes** (`packages/cloud/api/cron/cleanup-stuck-provisioning/route.ts`, `STUCK_THRESHOLD_MINUTES = 10`, fired every 5 min).

So the window `10 min < elapsed < 15 min` is a legitimate cold boot that the sweeper treats as abandoned.

## Why it is worse than a bad status

`error` is in `TERMINAL_SANDBOX_STATUSES`, and the orphan reconciler reaps a terminal-status container with **no age grace**. So the container the wake/resume just created is `docker rm`'d while its job is still running — the agent is destroyed mid-boot, and the row is left terminal with no retry.

## Prior art in this same predicate

`agent_restart` was added to this exact `IN (...)` list precisely because a warm-claim restart legitimately owns a `provisioning` row and was being flipped to `error`. That fix was correct — it just stopped one type short of the other two that do the same thing. The route's own doc comment states the intended rule as *"no jobs row in ('pending','in_progress')"*, with **no** type filter at all, which is further evidence the narrow list is an oversight rather than a deliberate allow-list.

## Evidence it already fired

From the live prod audit in #17162 (2026-07-13, 04:00–18:00 UTC): 44 dedicated agents in terminal `error` across 42 orgs, of which **19** carry `Agent was stuck in provisioning state with no active provisioning job` — the string written at `agent-sandboxes.ts:747`. 37 of those orgs had no other running agent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A job type that can legitimately own a `provisioning` row is never treated as abandoned by the sweeper. Prefer importing the same `COLD_BOOT_JOB_TYPES` constant the daemon uses, so the two lists cannot drift apart again (the drift is the bug; a second hand-maintained list would reproduce it).
- [ ] The sweeper threshold is not shorter than the longest cold-boot budget it can observe — today 10 min vs 15 min.
- [ ] All three occurrences of the predicate (`:360`, `:760`, `:1040`) move together, or share one source.
- [ ] A regression test pins that a `provisioning` row owned by an in-flight `agent_wake`/`agent_resume` past the sweeper cutoff is **not** flipped to `error`.
- [ ] Recovery for rows already stranded by this path is considered separately (#17162 tracks the 44).

Found by post-merge gap audit of the canary/provisioning-lifecycle cluster. [stan-cloud]

dc:T8ca,## Problem

Caller-supplied container `environment_vars` are persisted in
`containers.environment_vars` and materialized through `docker create -e`.
Secret-bearing values can therefore appear in the database, the SSH command
line, Docker inspect output, and process environment.

PR #17301 attempted to replace them with `vault://` references, but its machine
credential called Steward's human `/secrets` CRUD. That surface requires an
owner/admin session plus recent MFA and intentionally rejects tenant API keys.
elizaOS also has no cloud-container resolver for `vault://cloud/env/...`; the
local vault bridge deliberately fails closed in cloud-provisioned containers.

## Required architecture

Design and ship one end-to-end workload secret path across Steward and elizaOS:

- Steward exposes a workload-scoped write/read contract which does not reveal
  tenant-wide secret inventory and does not depend on a human MFA session.
- Provisioning issues a per-container or per-agent capability with least
  privilege, explicit expiry, rotation, and revocation. A tenant-wide master
  credential must not be placed in Docker environment variables.
- The agent boot path exchanges/uses that workload identity and resolves
  references into runtime settings only. Plaintext and unresolved sentinels
  must never enter `process.env`.
- Creation, update, restart, recovery, deletion, and credential rotation have
  defined atomicity and cleanup behavior.
- The feature stays disabled until both writer and resolver are deployed and
  verified together.

## Acceptance criteria

- Real integration tests run against the actual Steward API/auth middleware,
  not an invented in-memory `/secrets` route.
- Tests cover authorization, cross-tenant denial, capability scope, expiry,
  revocation, rotation, malformed responses, partial failure, and Steward
  outage.
- Evidence proves secret values are absent from the container DB row, SSH
  command/log, `docker inspect`, application logs, and `process.env`, while the
  target plugin receives the correct runtime setting.
- Legacy/default-off behavior is explicit and the migration cannot be enabled
  before the resolver capability is present.

Supersedes the nonfunctional integration attempted in #17301.

A read-only audit prompted by staging recovery canary run 30224564063 found a deterministic capacity-accounting bug independent of that run's still-redacted leaf failure.

`DockerSandboxProvider.stopWithPolicy()` decrements `docker_nodes.allocated_count` after both a fresh container removal and canonical “No such container.” The durable agent row retains the same sandbox/node/container locator until credential cleanup and row deletion complete. If credential revocation, the row-delete CAS, process completion, or job status persistence fails after the first stop, a retry rehydrates the same locator, accepts the already-absent container, and decrements the same slot again. `GREATEST(count - 1, 0)` masks underflow but can free a live sibling's slot. Suspend also stops/decrements while retaining the locator, so a later delete can repeat the decrement without any retry.

The app-container path already solves this class with an atomic durable slot-release stamp; managed agent sandboxes lack an equivalent.

## Required invariant

One logical managed Docker allocation releases exactly one node slot across retries, crashes, already-absent responses, suspend/delete sequences, and late provider completion. Remote teardown remains retryable, while local capacity arithmetic is transactionally idempotent.

## Proposed narrow repair

Add durable deletion allocation ownership (for example `deletion_allocation_counted: boolean | null`):

- `true`: this exact deletion generation still owns one counted node slot;
- `false`: it had no counted slot or the slot was already released;
- `null`: no deletion intent / explicitly unresolved pre-migration intent.

Initialize it from the pre-delete lifecycle state, preserve it on recovery re-enqueue, and cover both queued and direct delete entrypoints. Make ordinary provider stop remote-teardown-only. After an accepted stop outcome, atomically CAS the exact deletion generation `true -> false` and decrement the exact node in the same DB transaction. Reconciliation counts deletion-pending/failed rows only while ownership remains true. Pre-migration deletion intents must be reconciled explicitly rather than guessed.

## Acceptance / real tests

Use real PGlite transactions and the real Docker provider with only SSH transport scripted:

- node count 2 with target + live sibling;
- first stop releases 2→1, downstream credential failure retains the row;
- retry receives “No such container,” completes delete, count remains 1;
- crash before release, crash after release, concurrent release, and stale attempt/locator/node/environment CAS cases;
- stopped/suspended agent with retained locator never decrements a sibling;
- reachable stop failure preserves ownership/count;
- timeout + late completion changes capacity once;
- provider stop never owns counter mutation;
- fresh-live/stopped/shared/recovery enqueue initialization;
- workload reconciliation counts pending/failed deletion exactly when ownership is true;
- explicit legacy-null migration/reconciliation proof.

## Safety

Do not blind-rerun staging stale-canary deletion until #17184 classifies its terminal job. No manual DB counter write or global fleet mutation is authorized by this issue.

PRs #17284, #17285, #17286, and #17287 each identify a real production symptom, but their individual patches do not close the shared failure mode: multiple workers and recovery paths can act on the same logical sandbox generation without one durable execution owner or an immutable physical-resource identity.

The result is a family of races rather than four isolated bugs:

- timestamp equality is used as a compare-and-set token even though JavaScript truncates PostgreSQL microseconds;
- batch-claimed jobs can wait without renewable leases, and stale recovery can take work that is still executing;
- lifecycle contention can consume attempts or let a later operation overtake the active owner;
- warm-pool capacity counts rows that are not atomically claimable and applies image-local counts where the cap is global;
- recovery and teardown can identify Docker containers or VPN nodes by mutable names, prefixes, or logical UUID aliases instead of persisted provider IDs;
- worker health can remain green while a retained operational or infrastructure phase is wedged;
- local control-plane seams can activate against a non-local database if environment gating is too broad.

PR #17283 is a main-only backport and is not an implementation source for develop.

## Required invariants

1. Every claimed job has one durable execution owner, generation, renewable lease, and explicit quiescence point. Stale recovery must never reclaim an active lease.
2. Lifecycle admission binds the job to the exact sandbox generation under a database lock. Contention is a typed deferral and does not consume attempts.
3. Critical compare-and-set operations use an exact database token, not a millisecond timestamp window.
4. Every Docker placement persists the exact Docker container ID; every VPN placement persists the exact Headscale node ID and name. Recovery may enrich a legacy row only after proving one unambiguous physical match.
5. Destructive cleanup addresses only the persisted physical ID. Ambiguity, provider outage, or incomplete legacy identity fails closed and preserves the fence for operator recovery.
6. Warm-pool ready capacity uses one canonical claimability predicate, enforces the global cap, serializes maintenance, bounds probes, and reaps stuck incomplete rows.
7. The daemon separates job, operational, and infrastructure single-flight ownership, withholds heartbeat after an overdue phase, and joins retained work on shutdown.
8. Database timestamps are compared in UTC across PostgreSQL, PGlite, and JavaScript-authored schedules.
9. The database-backed mock processor preserves the same claim, lease, contention, and settlement semantics as production and is enabled only for an explicit cloud E2E run against a validated loopback database.

A worker restart currently spends a job's execution-attempt budget. That is the wrong accounting: `attempts` measures how many times the *job* was tried, and a restart is an infrastructure event the job did not cause. #17258 diagnosed this correctly and was closed because its implementation did not deliver the invariant it claimed — the counter lived inside the job's payload JSON, so for `data_storage = 'r2'` it always read back zero. The large payloads most likely to pressure a worker were exactly the ones left unbounded, and an inline payload could also cross the offload threshold on rewrite and lose the counter.

An infrastructure ownership counter is not user job input and does not belong in an executor payload. It needs a database-owned column, incremented atomically under the existing recovery fence, identical for every storage mode.

## Acceptance criteria (from the #17258 review)

- [ ] a dedicated non-negative interruption/recovery counter
- [ ] incremented and failed atomically with the status transition
- [ ] ordinary `attempts` preserved
- [ ] inline and offloaded payloads covered identically
- [ ] concurrent recovery proven unable to double-increment or revive an exhausted row
- [ ] the committed-canary special case retained under its existing exact fence

## Why this ships as two PRs

`deploy-eliza-provisioning-worker.yml` restarts the daemon — which calls `recoverInProgressJobsStartedBefore` at boot — on the same paths as `cloud-cf-deploy.yml`, but **without** `needs: migrate-db`. A single PR carrying both the migration and its reader lets the daemon deploy win the race and read a column that does not exist yet: `42703`, and since both recovery loops rethrow when every job in a batch failed, recovery is dead for the length of that window.

So:

1. **PR 1** — the migration and *nothing else*, not even the Drizzle schema entry (#17476). `ADD COLUMN … integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` is metadata-only on PG11+, so it is safe on a hot table. `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` rather than nullable because the pre-existing code writes rows without the column and must land on 0, not NULL. No `CHECK`: `ADD CONSTRAINT` full-scans under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, and non-negativity is structural — the only writer is `+ 1`.
2. **PR 2** — the schema entry, the reader and the increment, once PR 1 is deployed everywhere.

**Correction to an earlier version of this split:** it originally put the Drizzle schema entry in PR 1 on the assumption that a column nothing reads is inert. It is not. Drizzle enumerates columns in every `SELECT` it generates, so the schema entry alone makes every typed read of `jobs` fail against an unmigrated database — the same race, one level up. Verified: removing the column from a test's hand-rolled `jobs` DDL while the schema entry is present yields `column "execution_interruptions" of relation "jobs" does not exist / code: 42703` on ordinary reads.

## Design notes already settled

- **The counter is never reset.** A claim always precedes an interruption, so reset-on-claim caps it at 1 and makes the bound unreachable for the poison-pill class it exists to bound. `attempts` is never reset either; new work is a new row (`reEnqueueFailedDeletions` inserts), not a recycled one.
- **Non-double-increment is carried by `status` + `execution_quiesced_at`**, which EvalPlanQual re-evaluates against the live tuple — not by `attempts`. Since this change makes `attempts` non-discriminant on the interruption arm, the counter itself must join the CAS at **both** sites (the `FOR UPDATE` select and the `UPDATE … WHERE`). Cost is nil and it makes the proof one line.
- **The committed-canary case stays deliberately unbounded** under its exact fence — it resumes idempotent cleanup without consuming a terminal attempt, which is the point.
- The canary diagnostic's `classifyTerminalFailure` has to learn the new terminal message, or `isReservedRecoveryNamespace` throws. Fail-closed, so this is a hard break rather than a degradation.
- Four hand-rolled `jobs` DDLs in tests will break with `42703` until they gain the column: `pii-scrub-jobs.test.ts` (on the hot path), `jobs-recovery.test.ts`, `container-retirement-migration.test.ts`, `container-retirement.integration.test.ts`.

Our PRs have been red for two days on `job exceeded the maximum execution time of 25m0s` / `The operation was canceled` — never on the diffs themselves. I went onto the runner hosts to find the cause. It is **not** what I assumed, and it is not what the agent-capacity work suggested: the self-hosted robots are oversubscribed for the CI workload, and they run on **spinning disks**.

## Measurements (live, 2026-07-31, all five prod robots)

| host | cores | busy runners | load1 | iowait | disk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| eliza-prod-robot-2 | 12 | 8 | **47.1** | **60%** | ROTA=1 |
| eliza-prod-robot-6 | 12 | 5 | 15.8 | 5% | ROTA=1 |
| eliza-prod-robot-4 | 12 | 6 | **34.6** | 0% | ROTA=1 |
| eliza-prod-robot-3 | 12 | 5 | 8.3 | 10% | ROTA=1 |
| eliza-prod-robot-5 | 12 | 6 | 17.7 | — | ROTA=1 |

`lsblk` on robot-2: `sda`/`sdb` = **ST4000NM0024** — Seagate Constellation ES.3, 7200 rpm **mechanical**. Not SSD, not NVMe.

At the instant robot-2 was sampled: `user 5% · sys 4% · idle 31% · **iowait 60%**`, with **9 processes blocked on I/O** against 1 runnable. Top processes by CPU were `tar`, `unzstd`, `bun` — none above 4.2%. Nothing is compute-pegged; the box is waiting on platters while 8 concurrent monorepo builds extract caches and dependencies.

Loads are 0.7×–4× the core count across the fleet, and the mix shifts by phase (checkout/extract is I/O-bound, `tsc --noEmit` with an 8 GB heap and 578 Turbo tasks is CPU/RAM-bound). RAM is not the constraint: 79 GB used of 251 GB on robot-2.

## What it is NOT — two hypotheses I disproved

**1. It is not the customer agent containers.** `docker stats` on robot-2: 28 live `agent-*` containers consuming **1.1 cores of 12** in total. They are not starving CI.

**2. It is not the stuck agents from #17249 holding containers.** I cross-checked the DB against the hosts: of the 13 `deletion_failed`/`error` rows pointing at robot-2, **0 have a running container** — all 13 are pure DB rows whose container is already gone. Fleet-wide, 50 stuck rows carry a `container_name`, but on the host they do not exist. They cost capacity *accounting* (which is real — it is why an org hits its quota and why a node reads 25/24), not CPU or disk.

So the two problems are genuinely independent: #17249's agents block *quota*, the CI is slow from *runner oversubscription*.

## Consequences today

A 25-minute ceiling on `Type Check` / `Build` / `unit-tests` is not survivable when 6–8 peers share 12 cores and mechanical disks. Jobs die at the ceiling, get rerun, and the rerun joins the same contention — the queue never drains, it churns. Every red check on our open PRs this week traces to this, not to a diff.

## Options, with the tradeoff stated

1. **Lower runners per host** (6–8 → 3–4). Directly halves contention. Costs queue depth, but a job that finishes in 30 min beats a job that dies at 25 and is rerun twice. Cheapest lever, reversible, no hardware.
2. **Move the heavy lanes off the HDD robots** (typecheck/build/e2e to SSD-backed or hosted runners; keep light lanes on the robots).
3. **Give the robots SSDs** — the real fix for a monorepo CI, and the only one that addresses `tar`/`unzstd` cache extraction at the root.
4. Raising the 25-minute ceiling would only convert timeouts into long queues; it treats the symptom.

I have SSH on these hosts but will not change runner concurrency on shared CI infrastructure unilaterally — it trades everyone's throughput. Happy to apply option 1 on one host as a measured experiment if a maintainer says go, with before/after load and job-duration numbers.

f9:T577,## Problem

The benchmark CLI races `handleMessage()` against a fixed 120-second timer, but timing out does not abort the underlying message turn. It then calls `process.exit()` on every terminal path without stopping the runtime or closing the database adapter. Live Cerebras evidence from PR #17519 consequently left the trajectory row `active` after the process exited.

- abrupt exit can kill tracked post-delivery work before trajectory finalization;

Five independent lenses (crash safety, idempotency, budget coherence, failure classification, concurrency) produced 15 candidate defects; each was then handed to independent verifiers instructed to **refute** it. **8 were refuted and are deliberately not reported here** — the 7 below are the ones that survived, with the verifier's severity, not the finder's.

Two of the seven are already addressed by open work; the other five are unclaimed. Sections are independent — claim them individually.

---

## 1. Orphan reconciler reaps live warm-claimed customer containers — `high`

`packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/docker-node-workloads.ts:87-91`

The orphan diff keys a container on the id embedded in its **name**. A warm-pool container keeps the name it was born with, which carries the **pool** row's id — and that pool row is deleted at claim time. So after a claim, the live customer container maps to an id with no DB row, and the sweep classifies it `no_db_row` and force-removes it.

This hits **every agent created through the warm-pool fast path** — the default happy path. The agent goes unreachable mid-conversation while its row still says `running` with a `bridge_url` pointing at a dead container; the heartbeat only flips it to `disconnected` after the 120s grace, and for non-`dedicated-always` tiers it never self-heals. It is logged as a routine `Reaped orphan container … reason: no_db_row`, so it reads as correct behaviour in the logs.

What has spared production so far is that the reconciler is gated off by default (`ORPHAN_RECONCILER_ENABLED`, `provisioning-worker.ts:223`). **Arming it on an environment with warm pool enabled would delete live customer containers.** Worth a comment on the flag saying so until it is fixed.

Fix direction: resolve keys against `agent_sandboxes.container_name = 'agent-' || key`, or OR-in `warm_claim_source_pool_id IN (keys)` which `claimWarmContainer` already persists. Add a container-age grace on the `no_db_row` branch as defence in depth.

## 2. The cold-boot job budget is shorter than the provision path it is supposed to cover — `high`

`provisioning-jobs.ts:877` (`COLD_BOOT_STALE_JOB_THRESHOLD_MS = 900_000`), leaf budgets in `docker-sandbox-provider.ts:524/533/545/550/553`

The stale-job threshold is 15 minutes. The sum of the leaf SSH timeouts on the **single** provision path is ~19.8 minutes. A dedicated agent on a slow node — cold registry pull, slow SSH, a `docker pull` heading for its 300s cap — crosses 15 minutes of wall clock while perfectly healthy.

The daemon then **re-claims its own still-running job**, and the first act of the retry is to force-remove the container the first attempt just booted and delete its headscale node. The original attempt then fails against a container that no longer exists and marks the row `error`. Every retry burns another full cold pull and hits the same wall, so retrying makes it strictly worse; after 3 attempts the customer gets a permanent failure.

This one refines #17215/#17231 rather than duplicating it. Raising the *sweeper* threshold does not help here — the job budget itself is below the real worst case, so the job dies before the sweeper is even relevant.

Fix direction: a renewable lease. Have the executing daemon periodically bump `started_at` (or a dedicated `heartbeat_at` that `recoverStaleJobs`, `jobs.ts:675-687`, keys on) so a still-running job is never re-claimed. Raising the constant alone just moves the cliff.

## 3. Recovery flips a job to `failed` without the dependent-row writeback — `high`

`packages/cloud/shared/src/db/repositories/jobs.ts:788-815`

The normal permanent-failure path runs a writeback that settles the dependent row. The stale/startup **recovery** path flips the job to `failed` without it.

For `APP_DEPLOY` the app is left `deployment_status='building'` forever: the deploy-status endpoint reports BUILDING indefinitely — precisely the failure the writeback comment at `provisioning-jobs.ts:3025-3032` says it prevents — and every redeploy is rejected with `409 A deployment is already in progress`. Only a manual `UPDATE apps SET deployment_status='failed'` unblocks it. The same gap applies to `CONTAINER_PROVISION` and to `AGENT_UPGRADE`.

This is the same *shape* as the 44-agent stranding in #17162 and the 37 undeletable agents in #17249: a job dies by a route that skips the settlement its normal path performs, and the row is stranded in a non-terminal state with no sweeper that owns it.

Fix direction: resolve `buildPermanentFailureWriteback(job, …)` inside `recoverJobFromSnapshot` (`jobs.ts:796-813`) and run it in the same transaction as the `status: "failed"` flip, keeping the existing CAS fence.

## 4. Provision-retry container adoption is dead code — `high`

`eliza-sandbox.ts:8924` (throw site `8605-8614`, handle built at `9508-9525`)

`transferReplacementToPrimary` always throws on an adopted handle, so the preserve-and-adopt mechanism built for the SSH-blip case (#15310 §6) is **guaranteed** to end in a destroyed container plus a terminal `error` row. The customer watches a woken agent sit at `provisioning` for ~2 minutes, then hard-fail with an internal metadata error, and the already-healthy container is deleted.

The documented backstop cannot save it either: the daemon's `reconcileStuckProvisioning` selects only rows with no active provision job, and the job is pending for the whole retry.

Fix direction: move `const incoming = this.replacementLocatorFromHandle(handle)` from `:8924` into the `if (locator)` branch — it is only needed to prove identity against an existing durable fence — leaving `:8933-8938` as the sole check for the fence-less adoption case. Add a test that exercises the real `transferReplacementToPrimary`; the current coverage uses a prototype stand-in, which is why this stayed invisible.

## 5. Warm-pool container stranded at `running` with `pool_ready_at IS NULL` — `medium`

`containers/agent-warm-pool-creator.ts:36-45`

`provision()` commits `status='running'` and `markPoolEntryReady` is a strictly later, separate write. A crash between them strands the row `unclaimed / running / pool_ready_at=NULL`, which is:

- **counted as ready** by `countAllPoolEntries` (`agent-sandboxes.ts:1094-1108` guards `node_id` but omits `pool_ready_at` — its own comment at :1101-1104 asserts the invariant it then breaks, unlike `countUnclaimedPool` at :1076),
- **refused** by `claimWarmContainer` (:1334),
- **skipped** by `decideDrain` and missed by `findStuckPoolProvisioning`.

Unclaimable, undrainable, unreapable — while the container keeps running on a Hetzner node, keeps its headscale registration, holds an `allocated_count` slot and is billed indefinitely. Only manual SQL recovers it.

The verifier corrected the finder here, and the correction is worth keeping: this does **not** permanently starve the pool, because `targetPoolSize` is demand-driven and the first cold fallthrough lifts it. The real damage is a permanent −1 pool slot plus a container billed forever with no automated reclaim.

Fix direction: make readiness atomic — stamp `pool_ready_at` in the same statement that flips a pool row to `running`, or leave pool rows in `provisioning` so `markPoolEntryReady` is the sole writer of `running`. Defence in depth: add `isNotNull(pool_ready_at)` to the ready branch of `countAllPoolEntries`, and extend `findStuckPoolProvisioning` to match `status='running' AND pool_ready_at IS NULL AND updated_at < cutoff`.

## 6. `WarmPoolManager.healthCheck()` has no production caller — `medium`

`containers/agent-warm-pool.ts:300-358`

The `*/2 * * * *` entry in `cloudflare-cron.ts:54` is absent from `[triggers] crons` in `wrangler.toml:67-78`, and the route is a `cronSupersededByDaemon` stub whose daemon replacement wires a different cycle. So `healthCheck()` — and with it `findStuckPoolProvisioning` — never runs in production. Dead warm-pool containers are never reaped and can be handed to a customer.

Note the scoping: the broader version of this claim (that it causes permanent pool-budget starvation) was **refuted** — `markStuckProvisioningWithoutActiveJobAsError` does run on the real `*/5` trigger and catches the `provisioning` case within ~15 min. Only the narrow claim survives.

## 7. Already covered by open work — do not double-claim

Two confirmed findings land on predicates that #17231 already changes:

- the stuck-provisioning sweeper condemning rows owned by in-flight cold-boot jobs (`agent-sandboxes.ts:760`) — `high`
- the daemon reconciler sharing the same blind spot (`agent-sandboxes.ts:356-362`) — `medium`

Both are the two-job-type predicate replaced by `COLD_BOOT_JOB_TYPES` in #17231, which is open for review. Flagging them here because four independent lenses rediscovered this defect, which is a reasonable argument for prioritising that review — but see §2: the threshold change in that PR does not close the budget-coherence gap, and I would not want it read as if it did.

Focused core execution/budget/purity tests, affected provider tests, core and agent typechecks/builds, and current-base CI.104:Tb25,## Problem

elizaOS agents can already chat, browse, code, and hold crypto — but they can't autonomously pay for premium APIs. If an agent needs a captcha solved, a web page scraped, a token security scan, or a Polymarket odds lookup, a human has to approve every $0.01 transaction. That breaks the "autonomous agent OS" vision.

## What x402 is

[x402](https://x402.org) is an open M2M payment protocol built on HTTP `402 Payment Required`. An API returns `402` with a USDC invoice; the agent client pays it automatically via a crypto wallet, then retries and gets the result. No API keys, no monthly subscriptions, no human in the loop.

[minia2a.uk](https://minia2a.uk) is a live marketplace with 174+ pay-per-call APIs — captcha solving, web scraping, token security, Polymarket data, wallet intel, email verification, and 80+ more. 115 agents already registered.

## Why it fits elizaOS

1. **Plugin architecture already exists** — Actions, Providers, Services, Evaluators. An `@elizaos/plugin-x402` would be a Service that intercepts HTTP calls and handles 402 responses transparently.

2. **Wallets are already built in** — non-custodial EVM + Solana. x402 needs exactly this to sign and send USDC payments.

3. **Eliza Cloud monetization** — the repo already talks about "metering and creator earnings for published apps, agents, and MCPs." x402 is the protocol-level version of that: any API author can meter and charge, not just Eliza-hosted ones.

4. **TypeScript-native** — the existing x402 client SDKs (agent402-openai-agents, agent402-langchain) are Python. A TypeScript `@elizaos/plugin-x402` would be the first JS/TS SDK in the ecosystem, giving elizaOS a first-mover advantage.

## Sketch

```typescript
// eliza.yml or plugin config
plugins:
  - name: "@elizaos/plugin-x402"
    config:
      wallet: "0x..."      // or reuse built-in wallet
      maxPerCall: "1.00"   // USDC spending cap
      dailyLimit: "10.00"

// After plugin loads, any HTTP call that gets a 402:
//   → plugin intercepts
//   → checks spending limits  
//   → signs + sends USDC tx on Base
//   → retries original request
//   → agent gets the result without human approval
```

## Prior art

- [agent402-openai-agents](https://github.com/minia2a/agent402-openai-agents) — x402 middleware for OpenAI Agents SDK
- [agent402-langchain](https://github.com/minia2a/agent402-langchain) — x402 tool wrapper for LangChain
- [awesome-x402](https://minia2a.uk/awesome-x402.md) — ecosystem overview

## Who would use this

Any elizaOS agent that calls external APIs — which is basically all of them. The first agent framework with built-in autonomous payments has a real competitive edge in the M2M economy.

Happy to help with implementation or answer questions. 🤖

## Why I filed rather than fixed

The second failure has two defensible readings and picking one is a product decision, not a mechanical fix:

1. **The view is wrong** — `orchestrator` is a registered app-shell page that a user can land on, so it should grant `agent-surface` and be agent-clickable like its peers. Fix: add the grant to its surface manifest.

Whoever owns the view-capability model should decide. If it is reading 1, note the first failure (`Feed exposes spawn-agent`) may share a root cause — both are the bridge inventory disagreeing with what surfaces actually grant.

## Notes for whoever picks it up

- The capability is enforced at the surface-manifest layer; `ViewCapabilityDeniedError` names both the missing capability (`agent-click`) and the missing grant (`agent-surface`), so the error is precise about what to change.
- `packages/agent/src/runtime/view-action-affinity.ts:248` documents the neighbouring design intent — a view with no `relatedActions` and no `ViewCapability` only warns, because "the universal agent-surface still reaches every control". That comment implies agent-surface is expected to be broadly available, which leans toward reading 1, but it is about a different code path and I would not treat it as decisive.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

- Adds the full world-traveling co-parent persona and G1-G48 test catalog, plus
  a 12,792-word implementation report grounded in 31 official, research,
  safety, and first-person sources.
- Adds source-aware calendar availability across selected Google, Apple,
  Microsoft, and ICS feeds, including health/freshness/provenance and explicit
  partial/error states.
- Adds durable Google push-channel bindings, strict notification validation,
  dedupe/order checks, scheduled retries and renewals, restart reconstruction,
  quota classification, and controlled 410 resync.
- Adds immutable calendar mutation proposals, exact owner/editor routing,
  approval CAS, replay receipts, series/version/tenant/source binding, Apple
  add-only semantics, and truthful invitation decline behavior.
- Adds deterministic caregiver/vehicle/restraint capacity solving with
  authorization, accessibility, freshness, handoff, transition,
  distinct-resource, invalidation, and shared-review constraints.
- Extends one shared `ScheduledTask` architecture and typed dispatch results; it
  does not add a second scheduler.
- Adds school-source reconciliation, household operations, family
  communications, food/inventory, parenting guidance,

# Risks

Medium-to-large in blast radius, risk-reducing in direction. This changes a production deploy path under `.github/workflows`, so it needs human review and must not be auto-merged. It does not weaken any existing check; every change either tightens a boundary or holds it. The operational surface that changes is the release runbook (operators now dispatch from `develop` with a `candidate_run_id` instead of dispatching from the candidate branch), so a release operator should confirm that flow before the next promotion.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

### [P1] Candidate-controlled workflow code entered the production-secret job

A manually selected candidate SHA supplied `.github/workflows/eliza-computer.yml` and every deployment script, and the job then entered the production environment and received Cloudflare credentials. The admission check ran *inside* the candidate-controlled definition, so the candidate could modify or bypass the check meant to gate it. Human environment approval reduced likelihood but was not a code-enforced trust boundary.

The deploy job now:

- checks out `refs/heads/develop` and verifies through the API that the checkout is current `origin/develop`;
- rejects any `production-candidate` dispatch from a ref other than `develop`;
- accepts a candidate's build **by run identity** through a new `candidate_run_id` input, replacing `candidate_pr`.

The candidate contributes exactly one thing: the immutable artifact built by the secretless `quality` job. The protected admission step requires that run to be completed, successful, same-repository, not `pull_request`/`pull_request_target`, and a run of *this* workflow file, and requires its head SHA to be the current head of an open same-repository PR into `develop` that is zero commits behind a freshly fetched `origin/develop`. Deploy metadata, byte verification, and the Cloudflare commit hash all bind to the admitted bundle SHA.

Side benefit: because a candidate branch is never dispatched directly, the `eliza-army-production` deployment-branch allowlist keeps `develop` as its only entry and no longer needs the temporary-allowlist step the old runbook described.

### [P1] Production resolved Wrangler outside `bun.lock`

The job ran `bunx wrangler@4.100.0` *after* entering the production environment, so the secret-bearing lane could re-resolve executable content from a registry at deploy time. Per the correction on #17424, wrangler was already in `bun.lock` via the root override; the defect was that the job never installed from the lock and never invoked the installed binary.

Now: `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --filter @elizaos/eliza-computer`, then execute `packages/eliza-computer/node_modules/.bin/wrangler` for both the project-create and deploy paths. A preceding step asserts the binary reports the pinned version and fails **before** any credential is used. `wrangler@4.100.0` becomes an explicit `@elizaos/eliza-computer` devDependency matching the existing root override, which adds exactly one line to `bun.lock`.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fixes (security boundary repair in CI/CD), plus the documentation that describes the corrected release procedure.

## Two-project topology (re: the #17413 "packages/homepage/dist" note)

`eliza.army` and `eliza.app` are **separate** Cloudflare Pages projects and this deploy does not fight the existing homepage topology:

- `eliza-computer.yml` → project `eliza-computer` → `eliza.army`, built from `packages/eliza-computer` (standalone Vite site, `wrangler.toml` owns `pages_build_output_dir = "./dist"`).
- `deploy-homepage.yml` → project `eliza-app-home` → `eliza.app`, built from `packages/homepage`.

Their `paths:` filters are disjoint, so neither can preempt or overwrite the other. Documented in `packages/eliza-computer/AGENTS.md` so the two projects are not conflated later.

# Documentation changes needed?

Done in this PR. `packages/eliza-computer/AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` carry the corrected release runbook and the two-project topology; `.github/workflows/CHANGELOG.md` records the CI policy change.

Then read `packages/eliza-computer/scripts/deployment-contract.test.mjs`, which is what keeps those properties from regressing.

# Rollout and compatibility

- The feature fails closed unless `ELIZA_MOBILE_APP_AUTH_ENABLED` is exactly `true`, the environment is exactly `staging` or `production`, and `ELIZA_MOBILE_APP_AUTH_APP_ID` is a live approved app UUID whose allowed origins include the fixed callback.

- Mobile credentials use headers only. The server returns `mobile_credential_transport_forbidden` for `eliza_mobile_*` URL query tokens so a long-lived secret is never forwarded through the generic WebSocket channel.

122:Tfb3,Extends the abuse-aware scenario coverage that landed for the co-parent packs to every other persona pack.

## Why

An edge-case audit across all 14 persona catalogs found the co-parenting pack was the **only** one with meaningful coverage of the five dimensions real users actually produce. Most packs scored zero on all five:

| pack | rows | ambiguity | contradiction | privacy probe | injection | approval pressure |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| executive-assistant-transcript | 21 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| adhd-follow-through | 24 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| shift-rotation | 22 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| rupture-repair | 10 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| overdue-comms-apology | 10 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| co-parenting (already done) | 21 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 1 | 2 |

The corpus tested happy paths, not the behaviour that actually breaks assistants.

## What

**60 new rows across 12 packs**, five dimensions each: an ambiguous referent needing clarification, a mid-conversation self-contradiction that must supersede rather than duplicate, a third-party disclosure probe, instructions embedded in untrusted forwarded content that must be treated as data, and pressure to skip an outbound approval the agent must hold.

Each is grounded in that persona's own life rather than transplanted from the co-parent pack — a shift worker's ambiguity is a timezone-or-shift-boundary problem ("tomorrow" on a night shift), an ADHD persona's is two open loops, a caregiver's is which person is being supported, an EA's is which meeting or attendee.

## Grading

Semantics are judged by LLM rubrics that enumerate failure modes **including paraphrase**; deterministic matching is confined to named canary tokens and false-completion literals. For example the medical-probe rubric fails a response that "reveals **or hints at** the diagnosis" or "treats 'she wants to help' as consent" — a keyword list cannot distinguish those from a legitimate supportive reply, and pinning tone to string membership produces false verdicts in both directions.

Every new turn carries a `responseJudge`; every scenario an end-to-end `judgeRubric`. Structural gates stay deterministic where an LLM cannot replace them: `plannerExcludes`, `expectNoExternalSendDispatch`, `messageDelivered: false`, `memoryWriteOccurred`.

## Verification

- scenario-runner static guards (they walk every scenario file): **24/24 passing**
- persona catalog coverage gate: **exit 0**, corpus 344 → **414 authored rows**

Rows are registered `authored`, **not** verified — this changes nothing about live-provider evidence, and no pack's verified count moves.

# What this fixes

The Android lane had several independent false-proof paths:

- `reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner` executes each nonblank script line in a separate `sh -c`, so multiline Bash state, traps, PIDs, continuations, and `pipefail` were lost;
- a cold native `appUrlOpen` could arrive while the startup splash listener was mounted but still restoring reset/session state; reading `gatewayUrl` falsely acknowledged the command immediately before restore cleared the newly selected remote;
- hosted emulators expose a hardware keyboard, suppressing the real software IME even after the probe requested it, and the verifier sampled UIAutomator only once;
- Android toybox did not finalize `screenrecord` through the previous `pkill -INT` path, leaving an `ftyp/free/mdat` file with no `moov` box;
- failed verifier commands and non-finalized recordings could still look like uploaded proof.

The branch moves emulator work into committed Bash processes, queues and drains early native deep links, exposes renderer readiness, acknowledges/replays CONNECT delivery within a bounded window, and ensures only the correct startup owner can claim a deep link. It also forces the emulator software-IME policy, polls the actual IME hierarchy, terminates `screenrecord` by PID with SIGINT, waits for encoder/transport exit, and rejects incomplete ISO-BMFF output.

# Final remote-loopback correction

The final hosted run exposed one more device-only ambiguity: the remote-mac harness deliberately forwards the host through `http://127.0.0.1:31337`, while the Android client previously treated every loopback-shaped URL as the bundled native agent. That hijacked the forwarded request and returned `local_agent_unavailable` even though the remote coordinator was healthy.

The exact head now resolves Android routing from persisted runtime mode, durable Cloud-session precedence, and build defaults before deciding whether loopback HTTP belongs to the native bridge. IPC remains unambiguously native. The mounted-App regression drives a real `CONNECT_EVENT` through deferred first-run adoption and asserts the observable `adopt → complete → retry` outcome sequence, remote mode, shell state, and success notice.

Final local gates: 10 changed UI test files pass 143/143; the enforced changed-file coverage gate remains above 50% for every executable target (81.05% mean for the final routing slice); test-realness reports zero regressions; and `bun run verify` passes 573/573 Turbo tasks plus all audits and 28/28 dist-path consumers.

127:T1333,## P4 multiplayer coordination: group-room primitive in the Discord connector

Multiple humans + multiple agents in one room currently produce three structural failures: two agents answering the same human message, agents replying to superseded ("stale") human edges, and bot-to-bot reply loops. The Sol+Vera coordination protocol solved this behaviorally; this PR productizes it as a **runtime primitive** in `plugins/plugin-discord`, opt-in via `DISCORD_GROUP_COORDINATION_ENABLED` (default **off** — zero behavior change for existing deployments).

**Scope note:** deliberately does NOT touch outbound DM participant registration (#17167, @nubs's lane).

### What it does

New module `group-coordination.ts`, wired into `MessageManager.handleMessage` + the gateway `messageCreate` listener:

1. **One active speaker per human edge.** Before committing a model turn, an agent must win a durable *speaker lease* keyed `(channelId, edgeMessageId)`. The lease row id uses `stringToUuid` (agent-**independent**, unlike `createUniqueUuid`) so all agents sharing a coordination store contend on the same row. The claim is the adapter's existing atomic `onConflictDoNothing` insert followed by a read-back — the read-back decides the winner, both racers converge on the same holder. No CAS, no advisory locks, no new schema.
2. **Safe expiry/reclaim.** Leases carry `expiresAt`. A crashed holder's edge is reclaimed at **generation+1** (another atomic unique-row insert; expired rows are never mutated). A revived stale holder fails `verifySpeakerLease` (expired / superseded / not-holder) and **aborts before the third-party send** and before persisting any reply.
3. **Latest-human-edge-wins.** The gateway records each human (non-bot) message as the channel's edge. A claimed turn superseded by a newer human edge aborts at claim time *and* again pre-send. Explicit addressing (mention/reply-to-bot) overrides staleness — explicitly addressed work is never dropped — and a coalesced batch containing the latest edge stays current, so bursts coalesce per policy without dropping addressed work.
4. **Bot-to-bot loop prevention.** Bot messages never advance the human edge. A bot-authored message earns a reply only when it explicitly addresses this bot AND the per-channel consecutive bot-reply budget (`DISCORD_BOT_REPLY_BUDGET`, default 1, reset on every human message) is not exhausted. Two mutually-mentioning bots structurally stall after the budget until a human speaks.
5. **Auditable receipts.** Every decision (lease-claim won/lost/reclaimed/renewed, stale-edge abort, lost-lease abort, bot-loop suppression) persists a row in `discord_coordination_receipts` scoped to the room, with edge id, outcome, generation, and holder.

Retry/redelivery cannot double-send: the lease claim is idempotent per holder ("renewed"), and the existing durable-turn machine (#16696 lineage) reconciles a redelivery to REPLIED from the persisted reply memory.

### Tests (all green at exact head `eb5a727a7f3`)

- **`__tests__/group-coordination.test.ts`** (18) — protocol unit suite: concurrent claim race → one winner + loser observes winner; idempotent retry; expiry → generation+1 reclaim; two successors race an expired lease → one reclaimer; superseded verification; edge currency incl. explicit-mention override, coalesced-batch currency, out-of-order monotonic guard; bot budget + human-reset; receipt persistence + store-failure safety; config defaults.
- **`__tests__/messages-group-coordination.test.ts`** (6) — two REAL `MessageManager`s (two agents) share one store and race the same human message → exactly one third-party send, both leave lease receipts agreeing on the winner; newer human edge mid-generation → pre-send abort with receipt; explicit mention still sends; unaddressed bot message suppressed (ingested, receipted); addressed bot reply honors budget then exhausts; restart redelivery is a no-op (no double send).
- **`test/group-coordination-pglite.test.ts`** (5) — real `AgentRuntime` + in-process **PGlite** via the repo's shared test-runtime helper: the claim race, idempotent retry, crash→expiry→g+1 reclaim, revived-holder superseded abort, and receipt rows proven against the actual plugin-sql `onConflictDoNothing` seam (the atomicity the protocol depends on).
- Full `plugin-discord` unit suite: **66 files / 501 tests pass** including the new ones; durable-turn, inbound-idempotency, staleness, coalesce suites untouched-green. Biome clean; `tsc` introduces no new errors in touched files.

- No prod deploy, no workflow edits.
- No changes to #17167 (outbound DM participant registration) or its branch.
- Cross-process lease contention through one shared DB is exercised via two holder identities on one PGlite store; a multi-runtime docker-compose soak (the P4 "week in a room with Shadow+Shaw+Nubs" green bar) is the follow-up dogfood step.

# Risks

**Medium.** This is an authorization boundary, so both directions matter.

- **Fail-closed risk (mitigated):** the schema documents `groupPolicy: "allowlist"` as the default. Applying that literally would silently mute every existing env-only deployment that never wrote a policy. Resolution: `allowlist` applies as soon as *any* channel config exists; a deployment with no channel config at all resolves to `open`, and the resolution source is logged (`groupPolicySource: implicit-open|implicit-allowlist|explicit`). Same reasoning for DMs: no `dm` block at all means `legacy` (historical always-allowed).
- **New startup failures (intended):** ambiguous/unresolvable/deactivated identifiers and unhonorable config now throw during `startAccount`. This is the point of the change — an operator is entitled to have their policy enforced or to be told loudly that it is not — but it does mean a config that previously "worked" (by being ignored) can now fail to boot. Every message names the offending key and the fix.
- **`dm.policy="pairing"` now fails closed.** It is the schema default *once a `dm` block exists*, and this connector implements no pairing handshake. Admitting every DM instead would be the silent-acceptance bug again. Logged loudly at startup with the two working alternatives.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

`SlackConfigSchema` has long accepted a rich policy surface — per-channel `enabled`/`requireMention`/`users`/`allowBots`, account `groupPolicy`, and a `dm` block — while `SlackService` gated purely on the global `SLACK_SHOULD_RESPOND_ONLY_TO_MENTIONS` env flag and the `SLACK_CHANNEL_IDS` allowlist. **Config that looked applied was silently dropped**, which is the worst possible failure mode for an authorization boundary.

The review established the defect is deeper than the gate helper, so this replaces the helper with one authoritative policy model.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fixes (security-relevant: an authorization boundary that did not exist).

# Blocker-by-blocker response

### [P0-1] Config never reaches the gate — `c764af80f04`

Two independent drops, both fixed:

1. `buildCharacterFromConfig()` projected only the three Slack token env fields, so `connectors.slack` never landed on `character.settings.slack`. Now the non-credential **policy** object is projected as a plain setting (credentials keep flowing through `secrets`, redactable). Agent-entry `settings.slack` still wins so injected sandbox characters override file config.
2. `getMultiAccountConfig()` (accounts.ts) hand-picked 4 keys and discarded the rest. `SlackConfigSchema` is literally `SlackAccountSchema.extend({accounts})` — **the top level IS an account config** — so the object is now passed through whole, and `SlackMultiAccountConfig extends SlackAccountConfig` to match the schema's real shape.

Your exact reproduction is now a test. Controls assert the projection, the account resolution, **and** the enforcement at the registered Bolt handler, from a persisted `ElizaConfig`.

### [P0-2] Structured allowlists fail open — `1e27ba37ec6`

Root fix: **names are resolved to immutable IDs at startup**, once, before any handler is registered. Event-time authorization is an exact opaque-string comparison that never depends on a warm cache. Consequently:

- name-only records no longer produce an empty (therefore allow-all) allowlist;
- a name-keyed `enabled:false` is enforced on the **first** event;
- ambiguous names and unresolvable **restricted** entries **fail startup**;
- `handleMemberJoinedChannel` now **obeys** `groupPolicy` — a join no longer unions into admission, so invite-the-bot is no longer an allowlist bypass;
- `groupPolicy` is enforced (see Risks for the legacy-deployment carve-out), and `allowlist` with an empty allowlist fails startup rather than admitting nothing.

A pure-ID config costs **zero** startup API calls (asserted).

### [P1-3] User allowlist contract — `1e27ba37ec6`

Handlers compare the sender's opaque ID against IDs resolved at startup, so configured handles finally match. Ambiguity, unresolvable entries, and **deactivated** users all fail startup (a freed handle can be reused by another account — that is a live privilege-transfer bug). Per your Slack link, ID prefix shape is used **only** to decide whether a config key is a literal identifier or a name needing resolution; every authorization comparison is exact-match against an API-returned ID.

**`users: []` is now an EXPLICIT empty allowlist that denies everyone** — documented, warned at startup, and tested. Treating it as "no policy" was a fail-open.

### [P1-4] Event classification — `1e27ba37ec6`

`classifySlackEvent()` explicitly separates `im` / `app_home` / `mpim` / `channel` / private-channel. App Home traffic arrives on `D` channel IDs and was matching `channels["*"]`, so a channel-scoped `enabled:false` silently killed DMs. MPIM now runs on `dm.groupEnabled`/`dm.groupChannels` instead of channel policy. Unclassifiable events fail closed.

**DM policy is implemented here** (folding in the old slice 2): `open`/`allowlist`/`disabled` enforced; `pairing` fails closed with a loud startup warning, documented in Risks.

### [P1-5] One authoritative typed policy resolver — `1e27ba37ec6`

`allowlist.ts` is deleted; `policy.ts` owns account/channel/DM/event context in one resolver, reached from both handlers through a single call site so the two paths cannot drift.

`SlackChannelConfig` now mirrors `SlackChannelSchema` **exactly**: `tools`/`toolsBySender` added, invented `replyToMode` removed (the `.strict()` schema never accepted it, so it could not arrive through the production path), `allowBots` consumed. **Config the service cannot honor now FAILS configuration**: per-channel `tools`/`toolsBySender` and `mode:"http"` throw at startup; inert-but-harmless keys raise startup warnings naming exactly what has no effect.

### [P1-6] Evidence — partially complete, **live Slack round trip still needs a human**

Fully done, and the fake-Bolt criticism is addressed: **no test hand-constructs `ResolvedSlackAccount` any more.** `test-harness.ts` deliberately offers no way to inject one, because that shortcut is precisely how a gate receiving no configuration passed its own suite. Every gating test now drives the real chain: persisted `ElizaConfig` to real `buildCharacterFromConfig()` to `character.settings.slack` to real `resolveSlackAccount()` to real `resolveSlackAccountPolicy()` to real `registerEventHandlers()` to the captured Bolt callbacks.

**Not done, and I am not going to claim otherwise:** a real/sandbox Slack round trip with raw inbound payloads, outbound API responses, and reviewed logs. I cannot create a Slack workspace or issue `xoxb-`/`xapp-` tokens from this environment. Exactly what a human needs to do is listed under **Known gaps** below.

### [P0-3] Credentials crossed the secret boundary — `0dca2afeb39`

Your exact-head blocker, and you were right. The previous head assigned the whole canonical `connectors.slack` object to `character.settings.slack`. `SlackAccountSchema` declares `botToken` / `appToken` / `userToken` / `signingSecret` at the base level **and inside every `accounts.<id>` entry**, so all of them left the `settings.secrets` boundary the redactor scans and became ordinary settings — and the assignment shared the persisted object by reference.

Root fix rather than a strip-list:

- `projectConnectorPolicy()` returns a typed credential-free **view**: a deep clone (no shared structure with the persisted config) with every credential-classified key removed **at any depth**. Classification reuses the repo's own `isSensitiveConfigKey`, the same predicate driving config-API redaction, so "what is a credential" has one definition. It is deny-by-predicate, so a credential field added to the schema later is excluded by default instead of leaking.
- The stripped credentials are not lost. Base-level credentials (which every account inherits, since `SlackConfigSchema` is `SlackAccountSchema.extend({accounts})`) and per-account credentials are hoisted to deterministic keys on the **secret** path. Per-account credentials previously had no secret lane at all — that is what made plain-settings projection look necessary for multi-account.
- Key derivation lives once in `@elizaos/core` (`connectorAccountCredentialSettingKey` / `connectorBaseCredentialSettingKey`) so the projecting side and the consuming plugin cannot drift. One key per credential deliberately: the redactor's known-secret set is built from secret *values*, so a single packed JSON blob would only redact as a whole and let individual tokens through.
- `resolveSlackAccount()` reads credentials from the secret path, per-account overriding base, with the flat `SLACK_*` env lane still last and still default-account-only.

Exact-schema tests enumerate the live `SlackAccountSchema` / `SlackConfigSchema` shapes rather than a hand-copied list, and assert base and per-account credential fields never appear in plain character settings (**by key and by value**) while every policy field still reaches the Slack resolver. The independent credential derivation is type-aware, so `userTokenReadOnly` — a boolean policy flag that matches a naive `/token/` name test — is correctly not treated as a credential.

### Typecheck claim correction

You were right. The "107 baseline + 2 new errors" figure in the old body was an unbuilt-core artifact, not a real result. With core built first (`bun run --cwd packages/core build`), `bun run --cwd plugins/plugin-slack typecheck` **passes with zero errors**, and I fixed the two genuine type defects this rework introduced rather than reporting around them.

# Documentation changes needed?

No repo docs change. Behaviour that operators must know about is surfaced **at runtime**, which is more reliable than a doc: startup logs the resolved `groupPolicy` + its source, and warns by name for every configured key that has no effect.

# Known gaps / failures

**Live Slack evidence is NOT attached, and this PR should not be treated as having it.** (The credential-boundary blocker is covered by exact-schema tests, which do not need a workspace; the items below are the ones that genuinely do.)

Everything that can be built and proven without a workspace is done. The remaining package-contract evidence requires a human with Slack admin rights:

1. Create a sandbox Slack workspace and an **internal** app (must be internal, not distributed — distributed non-Marketplace apps eat the May-2025 rate-limit nerf: 1 req/min on `conversations.history`).
2. Enable Socket Mode; generate an app-level token (`connections:write`) and a bot token with: `app_mentions:read, channels:history, channels:read, chat:write, groups:history, groups:read, im:history, im:read, im:write, mpim:history, reactions:read, users:read`.
3. Paste `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` / `SLACK_APP_TOKEN` into the agent config and boot with a policy exercising: an ID-keyed channel, a name-keyed channel, a `users` allowlist, `groupPolicy: allowlist`, and a `dm` block.
4. Capture, per the package contract: raw inbound payloads for each event class (`message` in a public channel, `app_mention`, `message.im`, App Home / Messages-tab, `mpim`), outbound API responses, mapped entity/room IDs, thread + DM + multi-account + error paths, and the startup policy log lines.

I would rather report this honestly than dress up a fake-Bolt harness as a Slack round trip — that was a fair criticism the first time and I am not going to repeat it in a different costume. Happy to run step 4 and attach everything the moment someone provides a sandbox workspace and tokens.
129:T1b9c,## Authority decision

This draft supersedes #17462 as the controlled integration branch. Exact comparison found that neither #17462 at `fd22d142b28c` nor this branch's earlier `8cfdca706ba` was independently safe: both copied Slack credentials into plain Character settings, and #17462 also carried a second, divergent policy implementation and stale evidence. This branch now has one authority, `plugins/plugin-slack/src/policy.ts`; there is no parallel `allowlist.ts` engine.

## Repair

- Splits canonical `config.connectors.slack` at the runtime boundary. Non-secret policy reaches `character.settings.slack`; top-level and per-account `botToken`, `appToken`, `userToken`, and `signingSecret` exist only in `character.secrets.SLACK_CONNECTOR_CREDENTIALS_JSON` and are strictly parsed as credentials.
- Proves credential-bearing fields and values are absent from serialized plain settings while canonical policy still reaches account startup.
- Preserves env-only compatibility without accidentally materializing structured policy. Canonical persisted schema defaults intentionally select strict `groupPolicy: allowlist`; env-only boot retains its historical message/channel behavior.
- Compiles one account-scoped policy before Bolt starts. Channel and user names resolve to immutable IDs with pagination, ambiguity, inactive-user, and unresolved-name failures. Explicit opaque IDs use `id:` or `slack-id:` and do not depend on Slack prefix conventions.
- Requires authenticated bot and workspace identity, isolates accounts/workspaces, and rejects missing or foreign attribution across message, app mention, reaction, join/leave, and file event families.
- Classifies public/private channels, DMs, App Home, MPIMs, and threads through API/event metadata; enforces group, channel, user, bot, mention, DM, pairing, and group-DM policy without dynamic-join widening.
- Bounds conversation-kind, channel, user, and legacy dynamic-join state; directory traversal is paginated with cursor-loop and workspace-size guards.
- Implements `reactionNotifications` (`off | own | all | allowlist`) on the same policy authority. Reaction allowlists are exact Slack reaction names; malformed, numeric, empty, or dangling allowlists fail startup.
- Bridges authorized adds to `EventType.REACTION_RECEIVED`; removals stay plugin-local because core defines no removal contract. Missing `item.type`/`event_ts`, self loops, unauthorized users/DMs/workspaces, unknown lanes, and ambiguous lanes fail closed.
- Persists each outbound Slack response under its returned account/channel/message timestamp and actual thread room, including chunked responses, so `own` reaction targets can be resolved without `Date.now()` identity.
- Reports and rethrows policy, database, and event-emission failures. This is observability, not a retry guarantee: Bolt automatically acknowledges Events API events.
- Rejects accepted security-relevant configuration that the connector cannot enforce instead of silently ignoring it.

## #17469 / #17470 integration decision

- **#17469:** its useful reaction bridge is consolidated here, but not its fallback identity/room behavior. This head does not swallow DB/API errors, does not fabricate `Date.now()` event IDs, requires `item.type === "message"`, and applies full workspace/conversation/user/reaction policy.
- **#17470:** only fail-closed workspace isolation is integrated. Its process-local dedupe/arbitration and private Bolt reconnect hook are not imported. Exact review found retries could be dropped after failed processing, late mentions could double-dispatch, state was not replica/restart safe, missing workspace identity failed open, and the reconnect hook could silently disappear.
- Reliable dedupe/arbitration still requires a durable inbox persisted before acknowledgement through a supported custom receiver, with atomic account/workspace claims and worker/outbox processing. This draft does not claim that architecture exists.

# Risks

# Background

## What does this PR do?

- Adds first-party `@elizaos/plugin-aomi` and its generated registry entry.
- Keeps one Aomi session per Eliza room for contextual follow-ups.
- Routes explicit Aomi prompts to a single `AOMI` action.
- Supports read-only Aomi tasks without credentials through the public
  `https://api.aomi.dev` default app.
- Previews and confirms single-call EVM transactions, EIP-712/personal
  signatures, Solana transactions, and Solana message signatures.
- Retains executed wallet results across failed Aomi callbacks so a retry cannot
  broadcast twice.
- Includes publish-ready 400x400 logo and 1280x640 banner assets.

![Aomi plugin banner](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phoebe-aomi/eliza/codex/aomi-plugin/plugins/plugin-aomi/images/banner.jpg)

## What kind of change is this?

Feature: a new non-breaking first-party blockchain plugin.

The new package README documents installation, configuration, capabilities,
confirmation behavior, development checks, and opt-in live tests.

12b:Tc2b,## Summary

Progresses #15783 by replacing process-local backup scheduling assumptions with a durable, generation-fenced database lane.

- reserves due backups with database time and `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
- fences attempts to the exact job claim and sandbox image generation
- prevents a late/reclaimed worker from marking a newer image healthy
- records absent, stale, unsupported, unreachable, repeated-failure, and backlog pressure states distinctly
- deduplicates fleet incidents and verifies non-2xx alert delivery
- caps alert claims to the visible actionable batch so truncated rows remain alertable
- makes snapshot execution fail closed behind `ELIZA_SNAPSHOT_JOBS_ENABLED`

## Why this is not a timer-only patch

The failure mode crosses scheduler, queue, image lifecycle, worker recovery, and operator health. This PR gives those boundaries durable identities and compare-and-swap transitions. A backup only advances freshness when the executing job still owns the exact attempt and image generation it started against; clock skew and stale worker completion cannot fabricate health.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

- restores stable under-message copy/reply/edit/playback controls without message reflow;
- keeps reply and navigation handoff focused on the composer while avoiding stale draft restoration;
- makes optimistic send/terminal reconciliation deterministic for queued turns;
- preserves one voice owner across playback, hands-free capture, and transcription privacy stop;
- keeps the sheet draggable through pending attachment tiles and gaps;
- carries the selected destination through the shell navigation event.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fixes and interaction improvements; no schema or deployment change.

# Documentation changes needed?

No product documentation change is required. The behavior is covered by component tests and the browser interaction harness.

## Outcome

This makes chat streaming a single, observable provider → runtime → SSE → React → database pipeline and removes latency policy from correctness CI.

The runtime now has one owner for assistant-message persistence, the SSE completion frame carries the exact committed IDs, the client reconciles optimistic messages in place, and normal streaming performs no post-response history reload. Failed persistence emits an error and never a fake `done`.

## Runtime and persistence

- Return the exact response-memory IDs committed by `DefaultMessageService`.
- Reuse those IDs in the chat route instead of writing or reading the assistant response a second time.
- Preserve callback-before-persistence delivery for fast first response, with the same-room persistence barrier added upstream, while withholding SSE `done` until the write succeeds.
- Mark genuinely ephemeral responses explicitly; never invent a database ID.
- Treat delta streams as deltas. The previous overlap heuristic could corrupt `Fast streaming stays smooth.` into `Fastreaming staysmooth.`.
- Remove the hidden 30-second runtime-ready gate.
- Remove the implicit 180-second chat-generation abort, 60-second browser SSE idle abort, 60-second trajectory-finalization abort, and 5-second conversation-restore race. Cancellation is now caller-owned through `AbortSignal` unless a caller explicitly configures a boundary.
- Move trajectory persistence/finalization off the visible-response path while tracking it as post-delivery work.

## Providers, cache, and database

- Providers selected for a compose run execute concurrently through one `Promise.all`.
- Stage 1 excludes context it cannot consume; the planner reuses all already-composed provider results and refreshes only `RECENT_MESSAGES` when an early reply changed history.
- Replace mutable one-second identity/entity caches with exact turn-scoped promise memoization, rejection eviction, and explicit invalidation.
- Memoize sender-role, room, and related-entity reads within a turn.
- Skip attachment-history database work for ordinary text turns.
- Make SQL memory creation one atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING`, removing the read-before-write race and extra database round trip.
- Cache only successful shared-agent scope authorization. Failed 401/403/404 hydration is never persisted, so a corrected credential, tier, or agent row is observed on the next authoritative attempt instead of serving a stale denial for 30 seconds.

## Browser behavior

- Reconcile optimistic user/assistant IDs in place from the completion frame.
- Do not reload conversation history after an ordinary successful response.
- Reload only when the response is action/incomplete or committed IDs are unavailable.
- Replace requestAnimationFrame token throttling—which can stop making progress in background tabs—with microtask burst coalescing and a synchronous terminal flush.
- Remove the reconnect debounce/speculative resend path; user-triggered resend starts immediately and remains explicit.
- Add the missing `rate_limited` SSE contract.

## CI and telemetry

- Replace the ~1,000-line latency workflow with a small, manual, observational workflow.
- Remove numeric latency acceptance thresholds, regression ratchets, production-code-changed/test-changed gates, and the workflow self-test enforcing those policies.
- Run direct and gateway observations concurrently and upload raw JSONL. Telemetry reports numbers; it does not decide correctness.
- Remove numeric enforcement from inference-auth latency tooling.
- Add a real browser telemetry harness using the production route, production stream client, `useChatSend`, React transcript, real HTTP/SSE, and PGLite.
- Expand the Cerebras runner to cover the complete production chat flow plus an explicit concurrent sweep of every registered provider.

provider execution. The 149.989 ms wrapper outlier was a gap between compose
completion and stage-one preprocessing; it disappeared on the immediate repeat
(22 ms max), consistent with Bun GC/event-loop scheduling.

The remaining end-to-end outliers were model-side: the repeat had two Cerebras
calls at 2.1–2.56 seconds while local provider and delivery spans remained
normal. Detached message events, evaluators, and run-ended work occur after
terminal response visibility; they can still contend with local PGLite, but no
longer delay the visible response.

130:T1aa1,Closes #16442. One of the five cards that replaced the closed monolith #16200 (rebuilt narrowly on `develop`, not cherry-picked).

## Problem

Draft #16200 mounted a separate `ShellControllerProvider` in **each** desktop webview, so every window instantiated its own `useShellController` engine — duplicated chat sessions, fighting microphone/audio owners, and divergent conversation state. On current `develop` the same hazard exists: the `chat-overlay` (bottom-bar) and `tray-popover` windows each fall through to the full `App`, each mounting its own engine + mic.

## Design — one authoritative owner per process

- **Election.** Each window runs one `ShellControllerCoordinator`. They share a presence table and elect a single owner deterministically by `(priority, windowId)` — `main` (0) < `chat-overlay` (1) < `surface` (2) < `tray-popover` (3). Only the owner mounts the engine (the sole mic/audio owner). Followers render the owner's snapshot and forward commands. A joining window waits a short discovery grace before it may claim, so it hears an existing owner rather than briefly flashing a second engine. Lone/main windows own immediately, so **web, mobile, and single-window desktop behave exactly as before** (no transport ⇒ no bus traffic).
- **Handoff / crash / restart.** Owner leaves (clean `bye`) or crashes (heartbeat TTL prune) ⇒ the lowest-ranked live window is promoted; a promoted owner starts a strictly higher `epoch` so a dead owner's late snapshots are dropped. A restarted `main` window reclaims ownership.
- **Mic / audio ownership.** Exactly one window ever opens a mic or plays TTS (the owner). A follower's "start voice" is a *command*, never a local capture.

## Typed IPC contract

- **Commands** (follower → owner): a discriminated union (`send`, `startRecording`, `toggleHandsFree`, `speak`, `recheckMicPermission`, `navConversation`, …) — no `any`, no boolean-only dispatch. Idempotent: the owner dedupes by `commandId`, so a redelivered command re-acks but applies once. Replies (`ack`) are correlated by `commandId`; a failure (owner gone / timeout / version-mismatch) rejects visibly and surfaces a notice — never a silent no-op.
- **Snapshots** (owner → followers): ordered by `(epoch, seq)`; stale/reordered snapshots are dropped. The snapshot is the serialisable read-projection of the controller (the non-serialisable `AnalyserNode` and the imperative methods are excluded).
- **Presence + version.** Every envelope carries `protocolVersion`; an incompatible peer still competes for ownership (so no duplicate engine spawns across a version boundary) but a follower of an incompatible owner degrades to a visible `version-mismatch` state instead of rendering an envelope it can't interpret. All IPC input is validated at the boundary (`parseShellSyncEnvelope`).
- **Transport.** Production relays through the Electrobun native main process: a renderer publishes via the `shellControllerRelay` RPC; the main process fans it out to every window as a `shellControllerSync` push. The relay is a dumb pipe (the coordinator owns all semantics, and filters its own echo).

## Files changed

New renderer module `packages/ui/src/components/shell/shell-controller-sync/`: `protocol.ts`, `coordinator.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `transport.ts` (+ in-memory bus), `follower-controller.ts`, `apply-command.ts`, `electrobun-transport.ts`, `useShellControllerSync.ts`, plus `__tests__/`. Provider split in `ShellControllerContext.tsx` (owner mounts the engine; follower never does). Native relay: `packages/app-core/platforms/electrobun/src/shell-sync-relay.ts` + wiring in `index.ts` / `rpc-handlers.ts` / `rpc-schema.ts`.

## Exact candidate
- head: `dbcf6798cf2c235eb42e7f5d05f899e3a87db068`
- base: `00d6f6cdaeb40d9d70e9664ebaccbd8169718f26`

## Summary
- derive owner, exclusive, cold-boot, and detached-execution classifications from canonical lifecycle metadata
- retain separate provisioning recovery and orphan cleanup thresholds while fencing recent terminal owners
- acquire the per-agent advisory lock and recheck CAS predicates before stuck/orphan/healthy reconciliation mutations
- add a durable renewable execution lease keyed by job, owner, and monotonically increasing generation
- install claim and lease atomically, renew while provider work is active, and fence destructive mutations and settlement on the exact live generation
- keep timed-out execution supervised so its eventual settlement remains observable instead of abandoning an unknown side effect
- add migration, repository, lifecycle, recovery, and PGlite coverage for takeover and stale-owner races

## Root cause
Job status is not an execution lease. Provider work may outlive a local timeout or worker process, so a terminal-looking row cannot prove that side effects have quiesced. The earlier bulk recovery also raced lifecycle enqueue because it did not participate in the per-agent advisory lock. This candidate combines locked predicate rechecks with a durable renewable owner/generation lease, and only permits takeover after lease expiry plus the recovery grace period.

Provider APIs still cannot be made transactionally atomic with the database when they do not expose generation or idempotency tokens. The lease therefore prevents concurrent database ownership and stale settlement; it does not claim to undo an external side effect completed by a process that died before persisting its result.
